AT.note: Austria pays a lot of cash to families: universal child benefit, a €2,000-per-child tax credit and a well-paid, flexible parental-leave allowance (up to 80% of net pay for about a year). The weak spot is childcare: there is no legal entitlement to a place, only about one in three under-3s has one, and outside Vienna, Burgenland and Carinthia full-day kindergarten costs money. All cash benefits are frozen at 2025 levels for 2026 and 2027 (indexation suspended), so they lose value against inflation. On the labour side Austria is generous in kind rather than in rates: the 13th and 14th salary are taxed at a flat 6%, brackets are indexed against fiscal drag and parents in larger firms have an enforceable right to part-time until the child turns 8, but employee social contributions stay a flat 18% and there is no earned-income credit beyond the small Verkehrsabsetzbetrag.

headline.cash: ≈ €445/month for 2 small kids (Familienbeihilfe + Kinderabsetzbetrag, 2026)
headline.leave: ≈ 12–14 months Kinderbetreuungsgeld at 80% of net pay (max ≈ €2,400/month); 1 paid Papamonat
headline.childcare: no legal entitlement; free all-day kindergarten in Vienna, free half-day mandatory year from 5 nationwide
headline.tax: Familienbonus Plus €2,000/child/year off income tax (≈ €333/month for 2 kids)
headline.labourtax: 13th/14th salary taxed at 6%; brackets indexed to inflation since 2023 (+1.7% for 2026); €496 employee credit; no cut in 18% SV contributions
headline.workrights: 5 weeks paid leave + 13 holidays; legal right to part-time until child's 8th birthday (firms >20 staff); 2 weeks paid sick-child leave

policies.name: Kinderbetreuungsgeld (income-dependent variant) + Partnerschaftsbonus
policies.what: Parental-leave allowance chosen per child. Income-dependent variant: 80% of previous net earnings, max €80.12/day (≈ €2,400/month, 2026), for 365 days if one parent takes it, 426 days if both (61 days reserved for the second parent). Flat-rate 'Konto' alternative: €41.14/day for 365 days down to €17.65/day for 851 days. €500 bonus each if split roughly 50/50.
policies.value: ≈ €2,000/month for ~12 months per child at median net pay (≈ €24,000 per child); job protected up to the child's 2nd birthday
policies.eligibility: Parent in insured employment for 182 days before birth; parent must be on leave; earnings cap €8,600/year while receiving it.
policies.caveat: Daily rates frozen at 2025 level for 2026 and 2027 (indexation suspended). The reserved 61 days for the second parent are lost if not used; in practice most fathers take little.

policies.name: Familienbeihilfe + Kinderabsetzbetrag
policies.what: Universal monthly child benefit, no income test: €138.40 per child under 3, €148.00 age 3–9, €171.80 age 10–18 (2026), plus €8.60 per child sibling supplement for 2 children, plus a €70.90 child tax credit (Kinderabsetzbetrag) paid out with it. Extra €121.40 school-start payment each September from age 6.
policies.value: ≈ €445/month for a newborn + a toddler (2026)
policies.eligibility: All residents with children living in their household; paid automatically after birth registration.
policies.caveat: Amounts frozen for 2026 and 2027 (no inflation adjustment); a real-terms cut of roughly 3% per year.

policies.name: Familienbonus Plus
policies.what: Tax credit of €2,000.16 per child per year (€166.68/month) under 18, deducted directly from income tax; can be split 50/50 between parents or taken fully by one. Parents with too little tax owe get the Kindermehrbetrag (up to €700/child) instead.
policies.value: ≈ €4,000/year (≈ €333/month) for 2 kids, as long as the household pays at least that much income tax — true for a median full-time earner
policies.eligibility: Anyone receiving Familienbeihilfe for the child and paying Austrian income tax; claim via employer or annual tax return.
policies.caveat: Worth the full amount only if the claiming parent's income tax is at least €2,000 per child; during a year of parental leave the working parent should claim 100%.

policies.name: Flat 6% tax on the 13th and 14th salary (Jahressechstel)
policies.what: Nearly all Austrian employees receive 14 monthly salaries; the two special payments (Urlaubs- and Weihnachtsgeld) are taxed separately: the first €620 tax-free, the rest at a flat 6% up to one sixth of the year's regular pay (Jahressechstel), instead of the 20–40% marginal rate that would apply to normal salary (Steuerbuch 2026).
policies.value: At a median full-time wage of roughly €3,500 gross × 14, about €7,000 of special payments per earner attract ≈ €300 tax instead of ≈ €1,800–2,200: roughly €1,500–2,000 saved per earner, €3,000–4,000 per household per year
policies.eligibility: All employees whose collective agreement or contract provides special payments (in practice almost everyone); applied automatically by the employer in payroll.
policies.caveat: Social contributions (≈ 17%) are still due on the special payments; the 6% rate covers only up to one sixth of regular pay, so pay above the Jahressechstel is taxed normally.

policies.name: Elternteilzeit (legal right to part-time until age 8) + Pflegefreistellung
policies.what: Parents in firms with more than 20 employees and 3 years of service have an enforceable right to reduce or reshift working hours until the child's 8th birthday (max 7 years minus Mutterschutz and Karenz used), with dismissal protection; in smaller firms part-time must be negotiated. Separately, every employee gets one week per year of fully paid Pflegefreistellung to care for a sick child, plus a second week for a child under 12.
policies.value: Up to ~6–7 years of protected part-time per parent per child; 2 weeks (10 working days) per year of fully paid sick-child leave per parent
policies.eligibility: Elternteilzeit right: firm >20 employees, 3 years' uninterrupted tenure, child in the same household; Pflegefreistellung: all employees, both parents.
policies.caveat: No enforceable right in firms with 20 or fewer employees or with under 3 years of tenure; the employer can go to court over the requested hours; both parents cannot take Pflegefreistellung for the same day.

policies.name: Kindergarten: free mandatory year (national) + free all-day kindergarten in Vienna
policies.what: Nationwide, the last year before school (from age 5) is compulsory and free for 20 hours/week. Most Länder add free half-day places from about age 2.5–3. Vienna, Burgenland and Carinthia go further: all-day municipal and subsidised private kindergarten free from about age 1 until school; in Vienna parents pay only meals (roughly €80/month).
policies.value: In Vienna ≈ €0 fees for 2 full-day places (meals ≈ €80/month each); elsewhere roughly €100–€400/month per full-day place, more for under-3s
policies.eligibility: Vienna: child and one parent with main residence in Vienna. Mandatory year: all 5-year-olds.
policies.caveat: No legal entitlement to a place anywhere in Austria; only about one in three under-3s has a place (2024), fewer in rural areas; many rural kindergartens close at lunchtime or in summer.

policies.name: Abolition of kalte Progression (bracket indexation) + Verkehrsabsetzbetrag
policies.what: Since 2023 all income-tax brackets except the top one are raised automatically every year by at least two thirds of inflation (2026: +1.73% on 2.6% inflation; 2025: +3.83%), and credits are indexed too. Every employee also gets the Verkehrsabsetzbetrag of €496/year (2026) deducted from tax automatically, with a supplement of up to €804 for incomes below €30,259.
policies.value: Indexation is worth roughly €150 per earner in 2026 alone and cumulatively about €600–800 per earner per year since 2023 compared with frozen brackets; the Verkehrsabsetzbetrag adds €496 per earner (€992 per household); the supplement does not reach a median full-timer
policies.eligibility: All income-tax payers (indexation); all employees (Verkehrsabsetzbetrag, applied in payroll).
policies.url_label: BMF — Steuertarif 2025/2026 und Anpassung der Tarifstufen
policies.caveat: Only two thirds of inflation is passed on automatically; the remaining third is decided politically each year and for 2026 was not fully used. Employee social contributions (≈ 18%) are not indexed and remain among the highest in the EU.

policies.name: 5 weeks' paid leave, 13 public holidays, full sick pay and tax-free employer perks
policies.what: Statutory annual leave is 30 working days (5 weeks; 6 weeks after 25 years) plus 13 paid public holidays. Employers pay full salary for 6–12 weeks of the employee's own illness (by seniority) before health insurance takes over. Employers may add tax- and contribution-free extras: meal vouchers up to €8 per working day, a childcare subsidy up to €2,000 per child per year (under 14), an Öffi-Ticket and a €1,000 employee bonus (2025).
policies.value: ≈ 38 paid days off per year per parent; ≈ €1,900/year tax-free meal vouchers and up to €4,000/year childcare subsidy for 2 kids if the employer offers them
policies.eligibility: All employees (leave, holidays, sick pay); employer perks are voluntary and must be offered to all staff or a group.
policies.caveat: Meal vouchers and childcare subsidies depend entirely on the employer; roughly half of private-sector workers get no meal benefit. Leave in the first six months accrues only pro rata.

policies.name: Papamonat + Familienzeitbonus
policies.what: Fathers may take 28–31 days off work immediately after the birth (Papamonat, job protected) and receive the Familienzeitbonus of €54.87/day (2026) from the health-insurance fund; employer pays nothing. The bonus is later offset against the father's own Kinderbetreuungsgeld if he takes any.
policies.value: ≈ €1,540–€1,700 for one month at home after each birth
policies.eligibility: Employed fathers insured for 182 days before birth, living in the same household, fully off work for the month.
policies.caveat: About 55–65% of a median net wage, and it is deducted from any Kinderbetreuungsgeld the father later claims; rate frozen for 2026–2027.

official.label: oesterreich.gv.at — Financial support for families (English)

guide.label: MISSOC comparative tables (EU social protection, family benefits)

BE.note: Belgium (figures below are for Flanders, where child benefit and childcare are regional; Wallonia and Brussels run similar but separately priced schemes) gives this household a universal child benefit of about €380/month for two children, income-priced crèches and free kleuterschool from age 2.5, which cuts the expensive childcare phase to roughly two years per child. Leave is short and flat-rate after maternity: parental leave pays only about €1,000/month. The real constraint is supply: subsidised crèche places in Flemish cities have multi-month waiting lists, and rent support is not available at two median wages. Belgium's employee contributions (13.07%) and 45-50% marginal rates bite at a median wage since the werkbonus phases out below it, but every earner gets a large flat expense deduction and, on the non-cash side, an enforceable right to part-time tijdskrediet until the child is 8, 30 days' full employer sick pay and near-universal tax-free meal vouchers.

headline.cash: ≈ €381/month for 2 kids (Groeipakket basisbedrag €190.66 each from Sept 2026) + €1,311 birth grant
headline.leave: 15 weeks maternity (82% then 75%, capped); 20 days birth leave; 4 months parental leave per parent at ≈ €1,000/month flat
headline.childcare: kleuterschool free from age 2.5; crèche fee income-based, roughly €25-30/day at two median wages (max €35.89)
headline.tax: extra tax-free allowance €5,230 for 2 kids (2026 income) + 45% tax reduction on childcare costs up to €16.90/day/child
headline.labourtax: brackets indexed yearly; 30% flat expense deduction (cap ≈ €5,900) worth ≈ €2,400/earner; werkbonus contribution cut ends at €3,404 gross, below a median wage
headline.workrights: 20 days leave + 10 holidays; tijdskrediet part-time until child is 8 (up to 48-51 months); meal vouchers €8/day, employer €6.91 tax-free

policies.name: Kinderopvang met inkomenstarief + free kleuteronderwijs from 2.5
policies.what: Subsidised crèches charge a legally set day price based on joint taxable income: €6.47 to €35.89 per full day (2026), with a discount per extra dependent child; at two median wages expect roughly €25-30/day (~€500-600/month full time), 45% of which comes back as a tax reduction. From age 2.5 children enter kleuterschool, which is free (small materials bill only).
policies.value: ≈ €500-600/month for the baby in crèche (before tax reduction); ≈ €0 for the toddler from age 2.5
policies.eligibility: All families; request an attest inkomenstarief via mijn.opgroeien.be before the child starts; kleuterschool open to every child from 2.5.
policies.caveat: Places are the problem: Flemish subsidised crèches have waiting lists of 6-12 months in cities and the sector lost capacity in 2023-24; non-subsidised crèches charge a free market price (~€35-45/day), partly offset by a €3.78/day kinderopvangtoeslag. The fee scale is indexed +3.27% on 1 October 2026.

policies.name: Groeipakket (Flemish child benefit): startbedrag + basisbedrag
policies.what: Universal, non-means-tested monthly benefit of €190.66 per child born from 2019 (from 1 Sept 2026; €184.62 before), plus a one-off birth grant (startbedrag) of €1,310.75 per child and a small yearly school bonus, paid by a licensed payer (e.g. FONS, Parentia). A means-tested sociale toeslag stops at €49,024 gross taxable family income for 1-2 children, below two median wages.
policies.value: ≈ €381/month for 2 kids + €1,311 per birth (2026)
policies.eligibility: Every child domiciled in Flanders; no income test for the basic amount.
policies.caveat: Regional: Wallonia and Brussels pay comparable but different amounts under their own schemes. Indexed only once a year (September).

policies.name: Forfaitaire beroepskosten (30% flat expense deduction) + automatic indexation of brackets and tax-free allowance
policies.what: Every employee's taxable wage is cut by a flat 30% for professional expenses, capped at roughly €5,900 for 2025 income, without receipts; the deduction applies before the 25/40/45/50% brackets, which are indexed every year (2025 income: 25% up to ≈ €16,320, 50% above ≈ €49,840) together with the belastingvrije som (€11,180 for 2026 income).
policies.value: ≈ €2,400-2,650/year per earner (cap x 40-45% marginal rate) ≈ €5,000/year for the couple; indexation alone avoids ≈ €300-400/year of fiscal drag per earner
policies.eligibility: Automatic for all employees; higher real expenses can be claimed instead.
policies.caveat: The werkbonus (up to €127.54/month less employee contributions from Sept 2026) is fully phased out at €3,403.62 gross/month, i.e. below a full-time median wage, so it only helps a low-paid or part-time earner; the 2025 coalition's promised higher tax-free allowance and lower special social contribution (BBSZ) are being phased in gradually.

policies.name: Moederschapsrust, geboorteverlof and ouderschapsverlof
policies.what: Maternity: 15 weeks at 82% of gross pay for 30 days (uncapped), then 75% (capped), via the health insurer. Birth leave for the father/co-parent: 20 days, 3 at full employer pay, the rest at 82% (capped). Parental leave: 4 months per parent, full- or part-time, until age 12, at a flat RVA/ONEM allowance of €1,080 gross (≈ €970 net) monthly.
policies.value: ≈ 3.5 months at ~80% pay for the mother, 4 weeks for the father, then up to 8 months of flat ≈ €1,000/month between the two
policies.eligibility: Employees with recent insured work; parental leave needs 12 months with the current employer in the last 15.
policies.caveat: The parental-leave allowance replaces less than a third of a median wage, so most couples take it part-time (1/5 or half-time) rather than as a block.

policies.name: Maaltijdcheques, ecocheques and tax-free commuting allowances
policies.what: Meal vouchers of up to €8 per working day are free of tax and social contributions when the employer pays at most €6.91 and the employee at least €1.09; ecocheques add up to €250/year tax-free. Employers must reimburse most of a train season ticket and can pay a tax-free bike allowance of €0.36/km (2025, capped ≈ €3,600/year).
policies.value: ≈ €1,500/year per earner tax-free in meal vouchers (≈ 220 days x €6.91) + €250 ecocheques, if the employer or sector grants them (most white-collar sectors do)
policies.eligibility: Set by sector collective agreement or employer; roughly two-thirds of private-sector employees receive meal vouchers.
policies.caveat: Not a legal entitlement: depends on your sector or employer; the €8 maximum has not been indexed since 2016 (the 2025 federal coalition plans a rise to €10 over the legislature).

policies.name: Tijdskrediet met motief zorg voor kind (right to part-time until age 8) + 20 days leave, 10 holidays, 30 days full sick pay
policies.what: Employees with 24 months' seniority can cut to 4/5 or half-time (child under 8) or stop fully (child under 5) for up to 48-51 months over a career, with an RVA allowance (roughly €200/month at 4/5, ≈ €1,000 full-time, 2025) and dismissal protection. Statutory leave: 20 days plus 10 paid public holidays; white-collar staff get 100% employer pay for the first 30 days of illness.
policies.value: up to ≈ 4 years of protected 4/5-time per parent (≈ 20% pay cut, softened by ≈ €200/month) + 30 days/year of leave and holidays + full pay for a month of sickness
policies.eligibility: Employees in the private sector with 2 years at the employer; employers with 10 or fewer staff must consent; 4/5 and half-time also possible via the parental-leave scheme already listed.
policies.caveat: The 4/5 and half-time forms require having worked at least full-time / 3/4 in the preceding 12 months; the allowance is flat and small; paid sick-child leave is limited to 10 days/year of unpaid 'verlof om dwingende redenen' unless the sector pays.

policies.name: Verhoogde belastingvrije som for children + belastingvermindering kinderopvang
policies.what: Each taxpayer's tax-free allowance (€11,180 for 2026 income) is raised by €2,030 for one dependent child and €5,230 for two, relieved at the lowest bracket rates. Separately, 45% of childcare costs for children under 14 is refunded as a tax reduction, on up to €16.90 per day per child (2025 income; indexed yearly), covering crèche, childminder and holiday care.
policies.value: ≈ €1,300-1,900/year from the child allowance + up to ≈ €1,650/year per child in full-time crèche
policies.eligibility: All resident taxpayers; childcare reduction needs the yearly fiscal attest from the crèche or care provider.
policies.caveat: Only care provided by licensed/registered providers qualifies; the reduction is received the year after the cost, via the tax return.

official.label: Vlaanderen.be — Gezin, welzijn en gezondheid (kinderopvang, Groeipakket)

guide.label: MISSOC — comparative tables on family benefits (EU)

BG.note: Bulgaria (euro since 1 Jan 2026) gives a young working family two big things: one of Europe's longest earnings-related maternity leaves (410 days at 90%) followed by a flat benefit until age 2, and fully free public kindergartens and nurseries since April 2022. Cash child allowances are small and means-tested at a level (€466 net per family member) that a two-median-wage household only just misses or just meets. The 2026 budget froze the second-year benefit at €398.81 (a proposed rise to €460 was dropped) and kindergarten places in Sofia remain short. Bulgaria's flat 10% tax and roughly 13.8% employee contributions come with no earned-income credit, so beyond the child relief the only wage perk is the employer's tax-free food voucher of €102.26 a month; the labour code is more helpful, with 60 days a year of sick-child leave at 80% and a written right to ask for flexible or remote work until the child is 12.

headline.cash: one-off €191.74 (1st) + €460.17 (2nd child) birth grant; monthly €56.25 for 2 kids only if net income ≤ €466/family member
headline.leave: 410 days at 90% of pay (cap €2,300 insured income), then €398.81/month flat to age 2; 15 days paternity at 90%
headline.childcare: public nurseries (from 10 months) and kindergartens free of all fees incl. meals since April 2022; shortage of places in Sofia
headline.tax: taxable income reduced by €6,135.50 for 2 children → €613.55/year less income tax
headline.labourtax: 10% flat tax, no allowance, ≈ 13.8% employee contributions; only reliefs are the child relief and tax-free food vouchers of €102.26/month
headline.workrights: 20 days leave + 14 public holidays; sick-child leave 60 days/yr at 80%; parents of kids ≤12 may request flexible/remote work; paid breastfeeding breaks

policies.name: Обезщетение за бременност и раждане + отглеждане на дете до 2 г. (maternity and child-raising benefit)
policies.what: Insured mothers get 410 calendar days (45 before birth) at 90% of their average insurable income of the previous 24 months (income capped at €2,111.64/month, €2,300 from 1 Aug 2026). After that, leave until the child's 2nd birthday at a flat €398.81/month (2026). Fathers get 15 days at 90% after the birth and may take over the leave from the child's 6th month.
policies.value: ≈ €900-1,000/month for 13.5 months for a mother earning a median gross wage of roughly €1,100, then €398.81/month for ~10 more months; father +15 days at 90%
policies.eligibility: 12 months of insurance for general sickness and maternity; paid by the National Social Security Institute (НОИ).
policies.url_label: НОИ (National Social Security Institute) — maternity benefit
policies.caveat: The second-year flat benefit was frozen at €398.81 in the 2026 budget after a proposed increase to €460.17 was dropped; a parent who returns to work before age 2 keeps only 50% of it (€199.41/month).

policies.name: Безплатни детски ясли и градини (fee-free public nurseries and kindergartens)
policies.what: Since 1 April 2022 the state budget pays all parental fees, including meals, in municipal and state nurseries (from about 10 months) and kindergartens (from 3; preschool compulsory from 4). Families whose child gets no municipal place can claim compensation of up to €296.57/month (order of April 2025) towards a private nursery, kindergarten or licensed childminder, from 3 months of age until 1st grade.
policies.value: ≈ €0/month for two children in public care (private places cost €400-800/month); up to €296.57/month compensation if no public place is offered
policies.eligibility: All children with Bulgarian residence; admission by municipal ranking (Sofia: ИСОДЗ system).
policies.url_label: Sofia Municipality — kindergarten/nursery admission and compensation system (ИСОДЗ)
policies.caveat: Sofia and a few large cities still have thousands of unplaced 1-3-year-olds each year; the compensation covers only part of a private fee and requires a rejected municipal application.

policies.name: Данъчно облекчение за деца (child income-tax relief)
policies.what: One parent per child deducts a fixed sum from the annual taxable income: €3,067.75 for one child, €6,135.50 for two, €9,203.25 for three or more (2026 State Budget Act, same as the 2023-2025 levels). With Bulgaria's 10% flat income tax this returns €306.78, €613.55 or €920.33 a year, claimed via the employer in December or in the annual return.
policies.value: ≈ €613.55/year (≈ €51/month) back for 2 children
policies.eligibility: Resident parent with taxable income and no unpaid public debts; child under 18 and resident in the EU/EEA.
policies.url_label: НАП (National Revenue Agency) — Данъчни облекчения за деца
policies.caveat: The relief cannot exceed the parent's actual tax paid; a parent on maternity leave all year has no taxable income to set it against, so the other parent should claim both children.

policies.name: Еднократна помощ при раждане + месечни помощи за деца (birth grant and means-tested child allowance)
policies.what: Universal one-off birth grant of €191.74 for a 1st child, €460.17 for a 2nd, €230.09 for a 3rd (2026). Monthly family allowance until secondary school of €25.57 for one child or €56.25 for two, plus €102.26/month for a child under 1, are paid only if average net income per family member is at most €415 (full amount) or €466 (80%).
policies.value: €651.91 one-off for two births; €56.25/month (2 children) + €102.26/month (child under 1) only if family net income per member ≤ €466 — a two-median-wage couple with 2 children is right at that line
policies.eligibility: Birth grant: all resident mothers, no income test. Monthly allowances: income test, child attending school/vaccinated, applied at the Social Assistance Agency (АСП).
policies.url_label: АСП (Social Assistance Agency) — Семейни помощи за деца
policies.caveat: Monthly allowances are tiny by EU standards and the income ceiling (€466) rises only with the minimum wage; most two-earner families above the median receive nothing beyond the birth grant.

policies.name: Ваучери за храна (tax- and contribution-free food vouchers, €102.26/month)
policies.what: Under the Corporate Income Tax Act art. 209a an employer may load up to 200 lv = €102.26 per month per employee onto electronic food vouchers as a social expense, free of the 10% personal income tax and of all social contributions for both sides, provided the employee's base salary is not cut. Widely used since the 2022 doubling of the limit.
policies.value: €1,227/year per earner tax-free, ≈ €2,450 for two earners; roughly €290/year per earner more than the same amount paid as salary
policies.eligibility: Any employee whose employer chooses to grant vouchers (equally to all staff); employer must have no enforceable public debts.
policies.url_label: lex.bg — Закон за корпоративното подоходно облагане, чл. 209а
policies.caveat: Voluntary for the employer; usable only for food; the 2026 limit stayed at the 2023 level of 200 lv.

policies.name: Обезщетение за гледане на болно дете (sick-child benefit, 60 days a year at 80%)
policies.what: An insured parent caring for a sick child under 18 gets a benefit at the same rate as own sickness: 80% of average gross pay of the last 18 months (capped at average net pay), for up to 60 calendar days per year for the whole family (Social Insurance Code art. 45), plus unlimited days for a child in quarantine. The employer pays the first 2 working days of any sick note at 70%, then NSSI pays.
policies.value: up to 60 days/year at ≈ €880/month equivalent for a parent on a €1,100 gross wage; job-protected
policies.eligibility: 6 months of insurance for general illness and maternity; medical sick note issued for the child; either parent, one at a time.
policies.url_label: НОИ — парично обезщетение при временна неработоспособност
policies.caveat: 60 days is a family total across all children; own sick pay is also 80% (first 2 days 70% from the employer).

policies.name: Платен отпуск, гъвкава работа и кърмене (annual leave, flexible/remote work for parents, breastfeeding breaks)
policies.what: Labour Code: at least 20 working days of paid leave (art. 155) plus 14 public holidays (art. 154). A parent of a child up to 12 (limit raised from 8 in 2025) may propose in writing changed hours, remote work or other changes to reconcile work and family; the employer must answer in writing with reasons within 14 days (art. 167b). Breastfeeding: 2 x 1 hour a day paid by the employer until the child is 8 months (art. 166); 6 months unpaid job-protected leave per parent until age 8 (art. 167a).
policies.value: ≈ 34 paid days off per year per earner; 2 paid hours a day for the mother for ≈ 5 months after the 410-day leave; a written procedure, not an enforceable right, for flexible work
policies.eligibility: All employees; flexible-work request for parents of children up to 12; breastfeeding leave for mothers who breastfeed.
policies.caveat: The employer can refuse flexible work with a written justification; the 2 extra leave days for mothers of two children (art. 168) apply only if a collective agreement says so.

official.label: Social Assistance Agency — family benefits for children

guide.label: European Commission — Your social security rights in Bulgaria

CH.note: Switzerland is the weakest of the German-speaking countries for a young wage-earning family: high wages, but only 14 weeks of maternity leave, 2 weeks for the father, no paid parental leave at all, and childcare that costs CHF 110–150 per child per day before subsidies. Family allowances (at least CHF 215 per child per month) are the one reliable universal cash benefit. Subsidies for childcare and health-insurance premiums are cantonal and income-tested, so two median earners often get little; a new federal childcare allowance of up to CHF 500 per child per month was passed in 2025 and is expected from 2027. Wages are taxed lightly in Switzerland (about 6.4% employee social contributions plus pension-fund savings, income tax indexed against inflation and a two-earner deduction), but the labour-law floor is thin: four weeks' leave, no statutory right to part-time or flexible hours for parents, and only three paid days per episode to nurse a sick child.

headline.cash: ≥ CHF 430/month (≈ €460) for 2 kids (Kinderzulage min CHF 215 each; up to CHF 300+ in VS/GE/VD/ZG)
headline.leave: 14 weeks maternity + 2 weeks paternity at 80% (max CHF 220/day); no parental leave
headline.childcare: no entitlement; full cost ≈ CHF 110–150/day; cantonal subsidies income-tested; federal Betreuungszulage up to CHF 500/child/month expected 2027
headline.tax: federal deductions: childcare costs up to CHF 25,800/child, Kinderabzug CHF 6,800 (2025)
headline.labourtax: low wage taxes (≈ 6.4% AHV/ALV + BVG); federal two-earner deduction CHF 8,600–14,100; brackets indexed to CPI automatically; no earned-income credit
headline.workrights: 4 weeks paid leave + 8–15 cantonal holidays; no right to part-time; 3 days paid per sick-child episode (max 10/yr); 14-week paid leave for a seriously ill child

policies.name: Familienzulagen (Kinderzulage / Ausbildungszulage)
policies.what: Monthly child allowance paid through the employer's family-compensation fund: federal minimum CHF 215 per child under 16 and CHF 268 in education (since 2025, unchanged 2026). Cantons may pay more; Valais, Geneva, Vaud and Zug pay over CHF 300. One allowance per child, no income test.
policies.value: CHF 430–600+/month (≈ €460–640) for 2 kids depending on canton, 2026
policies.eligibility: All employees (and self-employed) with children; claimed via the employer; one parent per child.
policies.caveat: Amounts vary by canton of employment, not residence; the federal minimum has only been raised once (2025) since 2009.

policies.name: Mutterschaftsentschädigung + Vaterschaftsurlaub (EO)
policies.what: Mothers: 14 weeks (98 days) after birth at 80% of previous earnings, max CHF 220/day (≈ CHF 6,600/month), from the loss-of-earnings scheme (EO). Fathers/other parent: 2 weeks (10 working days) within 6 months of birth at the same 80% rate. There is no statutory parental leave after that; unpaid leave depends on the employer.
policies.value: ≈ CHF 5,400/month for 3.2 months for a median-wage mother (≈ CHF 17,000, ≈ €18,000) + ≈ CHF 2,500 for the father's 2 weeks
policies.eligibility: Insured for 9 months before birth and worked at least 5 months of that; job protected for 16 weeks after birth.
policies.caveat: Shortest paid leave in Western Europe; a mother who stops working after 14 weeks receives nothing further; many employers top up, but that is not a right.

policies.name: Cantonal/communal Kita subsidies + new federal Betreuungszulage (UKibeG)
policies.what: No legal entitlement to a place; a Kita day costs roughly CHF 110–150. Cities subsidise by income: in Zurich the parent share runs from about CHF 12 to CHF 120 per day. The federal UKibeG (passed Dec 2025, final July 2026, expected 2027) adds a care allowance of CHF 100/month per weekly care day, max CHF 500/child/month, until age 8.
policies.value: Today ≈ CHF 2,500–3,500/month net for 2 kids at 3 days/week for two median earners (small or no subsidy); from ~2027 minus up to CHF 600/month Betreuungszulage
policies.eligibility: Subsidies: residents of the commune, both parents working, income below cantonal ceilings. Betreuungszulage: child in a licensed crèche, daycare family or after-school care.
policies.caveat: Subsidy ceilings differ by commune and often phase out around a two-earner median income; waiting lists in cities; the federal allowance's start date is not yet fixed.

policies.name: Federal and cantonal child tax deductions
policies.what: Direct federal tax (tax year 2025): documented third-party childcare costs deductible up to CHF 25,800 per child under 14; general child deduction CHF 6,800 per child; CHF 263 per child off the tax bill (Elterntarif); extra insurance deduction per child. Cantons grant their own, usually smaller, childcare and child deductions.
policies.value: Roughly CHF 1,000–3,000/year less tax for 2 kids in full-time paid childcare, depending on canton and income
policies.eligibility: All taxpayers with dependent children; childcare deduction requires both parents working (or in training) and receipts.
policies.caveat: Federal tax is a small share of Swiss income tax; the big cantonal deductions vary from about CHF 10,000 to 25,000 for childcare.

policies.name: Paid sick-child leave (Art. 329h OR) + 14-week Betreuungsurlaub + paid breastfeeding breaks
policies.what: Since 2021 every employee may take paid leave to care for a sick child or relative: up to 3 days per episode and 10 days per year (Art. 329h OR; a doctor's note can be required). Parents of a seriously ill or injured child get a shared 14-week Betreuungsurlaub within 18 months, paid by the EO at 80% of income up to CHF 220/day. Mothers in their child's first year get paid breastfeeding time: 30, 60 or 90 minutes per day depending on hours worked.
policies.value: Up to 10 paid days per year per parent for ordinary child illness; in a serious case 14 weeks at ≈ CHF 5,400/month (median wage); ≈ 1 paid hour per working day for a breastfeeding mother
policies.eligibility: All employees (sick-child days); Betreuungsurlaub requires a medical certificate of serious health impairment and applies to both employed and self-employed parents.
policies.caveat: The 3-day/10-day rule is tight for a family with two small children in crèche; beyond it parents must use holidays or unpaid leave. The 14-week leave is for grave illness only, not for ordinary infections.

policies.name: Zweiverdienerabzug, professional-expense deduction and automatic bracket indexation (direct federal tax)
policies.what: Married two-earner couples deduct 50% of the lower income, at least CHF 8,600 and at most CHF 14,100 (2026), from federal taxable income; each earner also deducts 3% of net salary (CHF 2,000–4,000) for job costs and up to CHF 25,800 per child of documented childcare. Federal brackets and deductions are indexed to the CPI every year by law (Art. 39 DBG; the 2026 index rose only 0.06%, so no shift). Most cantons grant a similar two-earner deduction.
policies.value: Roughly CHF 1,000–2,000 (≈ €1,050–2,100) less tax per year for two median earners (federal + cantonal two-earner deductions), plus ≈ CHF 4,900 of job-cost deductions; indexation prevents fiscal drag but was worth almost nothing for 2026
policies.eligibility: Two-earner deduction: married or registered couples where both work (unmarried couples are taxed individually anyway); job-cost lump sum: all employees.
policies.url_label: ESTV — Rundschreiben Nr. 215: kalte Progression und Abzüge Steuerjahr 2026
policies.caveat: Despite the deduction, married two-earner couples still pay more federal tax than an unmarried couple with the same income (the 'Heiratsstrafe'); a switch to individual taxation adopted by Parliament in 2025 is contested by referendum and would apply from about 2028 at the earliest. Cantonal rules differ widely.

policies.name: Prämienverbilligung for children's health-insurance premiums
policies.what: Health insurance is compulsory and paid per person, including children (average child premium about CHF 120/month in 2026). Cantons must reduce children's premiums by at least 80% for families with lower and middle incomes, and reduce adults' premiums on a sliding scale; thresholds and procedures are cantonal.
policies.value: Up to ≈ CHF 200/month saved on 2 children's premiums if the household is under the cantonal ceiling
policies.eligibility: Set by each canton on taxable income and household size; some cantons pay automatically, others require an application.
policies.caveat: A two-median-earner family qualifies in some cantons and not in others; premiums rose 4.4% on average for 2026.

policies.name: 4 weeks' paid leave, cantonal public holidays, employer sick pay — but no right to part-time
policies.what: The Code of Obligations guarantees 4 weeks' paid holiday (5 weeks under age 20); many employers give 5. Public holidays: 1 August federally plus 8–14 cantonal days (e.g. about 13 in Zurich, 9 in Geneva). Sick pay: the employer must pay full salary for at least 3 weeks in the first year of service and longer afterwards (cantonal scales); most employers insure daily sickness benefit at 80% for 720 days. There is no statutory right to part-time or flexible hours; the Labour Act only obliges employers to 'take account of' family duties and lets parents refuse overtime.
policies.value: ≈ 29–34 paid days off per year per parent; full pay for 3 weeks to several months of own illness; part-time only by agreement
policies.eligibility: All employees under private law; public-sector staff usually have better terms.
policies.caveat: Switzerland has the lowest statutory leave in Western Europe and no legal lever to reduce hours after parental leave; a parent who wants part-time depends entirely on the employer's goodwill. Holidays vary by canton.

CY.note: Cyprus has built its family package quickly since 2022: 22 weeks of maternity allowance at 72–80% of earnings, 8 paid weeks of parental leave per parent, an EU-funded nursery subsidy for under-4s and, from 2026, a higher tax-free threshold with per-child deductions. Ongoing cash is modest and means-tested: a dual-median-income couple (≈ €51,000 gross, CYSTAT median €1,968/month) sits in the lowest child-benefit band and loses it entirely above €59,000. There is no legal childcare entitlement before compulsory pre-primary (entry age being lowered from 4y8m towards 4 by 2032/33); nursery capacity and fees vary, and there is no rent support at this income. Wage taxation in Cyprus is already light for a median earner (employee contributions of 11.45% are tax-deductible and most pay falls under the €22,000 threshold), but the non-monetary side is thin: parents get only a right to request flexible work, unpaid emergency days and no employer-paid sick leave.

headline.cash: ≈ €75/month child benefit for 2 kids at ~€50k income (2026), €1,095 + €1,643 birth grants
headline.leave: 22 weeks maternity at 72–80% of earnings; 2 weeks paternity; 8 paid weeks parental leave per parent
headline.childcare: nursery subsidy €100–350/child/month (up to 80% of fees) for child-benefit families; free pre-primary from ~4.5
headline.tax: 2026 reform: tax-free €22,000 (was €19,500), €1,000 + €1,250 child deductions per parent, up to €2,000 rent deduction
headline.labourtax: 8.8% SI + 2.65% GHS employee contributions, tax-deductible (≈ €580/yr saved at median wage); no earned-income credit; 20% exemption if hired from abroad
headline.workrights: 4 weeks paid leave + ~14 customary holidays; flexible-work request until child is 15 (6 months' service); 7 unpaid force-majeure days; no employer sick pay

policies.name: Nursery/kindergarten tuition subsidy for children up to 4 (Deputy Ministry of Social Welfare)
policies.what: Since 2024/25 an EU Recovery-funded scheme pays up to 80% of monthly nursery fees for under-4s enrolled in a participating public or private nursery: €100–€350 per child per month depending on family income and number of children, paid to families that receive child benefit. A second scheme pays 100% of fees (cap €130 public / €200 private per month) for 4-year-olds until they enter free compulsory pre-primary. 2026/27 applications opened 7 September 2026.
policies.value: roughly €100–€200 per child per month at ~€50,000 income (≈ €2,400–4,800/yr for 2 kids); up to €350/child for lower incomes
policies.eligibility: Families entitled to child benefit for the year (income ≤ €59,000 with 2 children); child enrolled in a nursery that joined the scheme.
policies.url_label: gov.cy — Tuition subsidy for children up to 4 (parents)
policies.caveat: Annual, budget-limited scheme (~25,000 children, €22m); tied to the child-benefit income cut-off, so a pay rise above €59,000 removes both. Free compulsory pre-primary currently starts at 4 years 6 months (2025/26), reaching age 4 only by 2032/33.

policies.name: Maternity allowance (22 weeks) + paternity allowance + paid parental leave
policies.what: Social Insurance pays maternity allowance for 22 weeks for a first or second child (26 weeks from the third) at 72% of insurable earnings, rising to 80% with one dependant and 90% with two. Fathers get 2 consecutive weeks of paternity allowance on the same basis. Each parent also has 18 weeks of parental leave per child, of which 8 weeks are paid at 72% (max 5 weeks per year since 2025), usable until the child is 15.
policies.value: ≈ €8,000–9,000 maternity pay on a €2,000/month wage, ≈ €700 paternity, plus ≈ €2,900 per parent for the 8 paid parental-leave weeks
policies.eligibility: Insured employees and self-employed with at least 26 weeks of contributions; parental-leave allowance needs 12 months' work in the last 2 years.
policies.url_label: Social Insurance Services — maternity, paternity and parental-leave allowances
policies.caveat: Employers are not obliged to top up to full pay; the remaining 10 weeks of parental leave are unpaid; fathers report multi-month processing waits.

policies.name: Child benefit (Επίδομα τέκνου) + childbirth grant
policies.what: Annual means-tested child benefit from the Welfare Benefits Administration Service. For 2 children (2025 table) it is €718 per child if family income is ≤ €19,500, €655 up to €39,000, €479 up to €49,000 and €435 up to €59,000, nothing above; 2026 bands are indexed (≈ €705/€643 in the lower bands, cut-offs €21,500/€41,000). Childbirth grant from Social Insurance: €1,095 for the first child, €1,643 for the second (2026).
policies.value: ≈ €870–960/yr (≈ €75/month) for 2 children at ~€50,000 income + €2,738 in birth grants over two births
policies.eligibility: Residents; family income ≤ €59,000 with 2 children (≤ €49,000 with one); assets ≤ €1.2m; birth grant needs 26 weeks of insurance by mother or father.
policies.url_label: gov.cy — Child benefit and single-parent family benefit
policies.caveat: Sharp cliff-edge at €59,000 for a 2-child family. A reform approved by Cabinet in September 2026 for January 2027 raises payments by 10% (income ≤ €22,000) or 5% (≤ €44,000) and widens thresholds mainly for families with 3+ children; it still needs Parliament.

policies.name: 2026 tax reform: higher tax-free threshold + child and rent deductions
policies.what: From 1 January 2026 the personal tax-free threshold rose from €19,500 to €22,000 (then 20% to €32,000, 25% to €42,000, 30% to €72,000, 35% above). New deductions per parent: €1,000 for the first child and €1,250 for the second (family income ≤ €100,000), plus up to €2,000 a year for rent or mortgage interest on the main home.
policies.value: roughly €900–1,500/yr less income tax for a dual-earner couple with 2 children versus 2025
policies.eligibility: All resident taxpayers; child deductions per parent within the income bands; rent deduction for the main residence.
policies.caveat: Deductions are worth only their marginal rate (20% for most median earners), and a parent earning under €22,000 gets nothing from them.

policies.name: Tax deductibility of employee social-insurance and GHS contributions
policies.what: Employee social-insurance contributions (8.8% of insurable earnings, rate fixed until 2029) and General Healthcare System contributions (2.65%) are deducted from taxable income before the personal tax scale is applied; together with provident-fund and life-insurance premiums the deduction is capped at 1/5 of net income. Tax is then charged at 20% only on income above €22,000 (2026).
policies.value: ≈ €580/yr less income tax per earner at €25,500 gross (≈ €1,170 per household); leaves a median earner paying roughly €120 income tax a year
policies.eligibility: All employees whose contributions are withheld by the employer; applied automatically in the TaxisNet return (the SI amount is pre-filled from the employer's certificate).
policies.url_label: Tax Department — Guide for the 2025 income-tax return for individuals (deductions, section C)
policies.caveat: There is no earned-income tax credit and contributions themselves are not reduced; the 8.8% social-insurance rate is legislated to rise to 9.3% in 2029.

policies.name: Paid annual leave + flexible-work request and unpaid family leave (Work-Life Balance law 2022)
policies.what: 4 weeks' paid annual leave after 48 weeks of work (20 days on a 5-day week, 24 on 6 days), paid by the employer or the Central Holiday Fund; around 14 public holidays are observed under collective agreements. Working parents of children up to 15 and carers with 6 months' service may request flexible arrangements (remote work, adapted hours, reduced hours). Also 7 unpaid force-majeure days and 5 unpaid carers' days a year; for 9 months after maternity leave the mother may take one paid hour off per day.
policies.value: 20 paid leave days (≈ €2,000 of paid time at €25,500/yr) + ~14 holidays; up to 12 unpaid family-emergency days a year
policies.eligibility: All private- and public-sector employees; flexible-work request and parental/carer leave need 6 months' continuous service with the employer.
policies.url_label: Department of Labour Relations — Work-life balance for parents and carers
policies.caveat: The employer may postpone or refuse a flexible-work request on business grounds; public holidays are not a statutory private-sector right. There is no employer-paid sick leave: own illness is covered only by the Social Insurance sickness benefit from the 4th day at about 60% of basic insurable earnings, unless a collective or individual agreement says otherwise.

policies.name: 20% income-tax exemption for people taking up first employment in Cyprus (art. 8(21A))
policies.what: Anyone who was employed outside Cyprus for at least 3 consecutive years before starting a job in Cyprus (employment begun from 26 July 2022) may exempt 20% of employment income, capped at €8,550 a year, for 7 years starting the January after the job began. A separate 50% exemption for 17 years applies only above €55,000 after 10 years abroad.
policies.value: up to ≈ €700/yr per earner at €25,500 gross (the exemption wipes out the tax on income above €22,000) for 7 years
policies.eligibility: Employees, of any nationality, who worked abroad for 3 consecutive years before their first Cypriot employment; claimed in the annual TaxisNet return (code 14).
policies.url_label: Tax Department — Guide for the 2025 income-tax return (employment income codes 3, 12, 14)
policies.caveat: Irrelevant for parents who already worked in Cyprus; worth little at a wage near the €22,000 threshold; the older 8(21) 20% rule (jobs started before 26 July 2022) ran for only 5 years.

CZ.note: Czechia gives a big, flexible lump of money per child (350,000 CZK parental allowance, drawn over up to 3 years while the parent may keep working) and a refundable child tax credit, but there is no universal child benefit any more: since 2025/26 the old child allowance and housing allowance were folded into one means-tested 'superdávka' that a two-earner median household is usually just above. Public kindergarten from age 3 is cheap and a place is guaranteed, but care for under-3s is scarce and expensive. Renters get no help unless income falls below the superdávka line. Labour taxation is flat and unindexed (15% PIT, 11.6% employee contributions, credits frozen since 2022), with one parent-specific break — the 24,840 CZK spouse credit while one partner is home with a child under 3; the work-rights side is stronger on paper, with a statutory claim to shorter hours until the child is 15, near-universal tax-free meal allowances, and 60% sick pay from day one.

headline.cash: 350,000 CZK (≈ €14,300) parental allowance per child, drawn flexibly until age 3; no universal monthly child benefit
headline.leave: 28 weeks maternity at 70% (≈ 27,000 CZK/month at median wage); 2 weeks paternity at 70%; father may take maternity benefit from week 7
headline.childcare: kindergarten: guaranteed place from age 3, fee max 8% of minimum wage (≤ 1,792 CZK/month, 2026), free last year; under-3 care scarce
headline.tax: refundable child tax credit 15,204 + 22,320 CZK/year for two children (≈ 3,100 CZK/month, ≈ €128)
headline.labourtax: 15% flat PIT above a 30,840 CZK basic credit; 24,840 CZK spouse credit while a partner stays home with a child under 3; employee contributions 11.6%; nothing indexed
headline.workrights: 4 weeks leave + 13 holidays; employer must grant shorter hours to parents of under-15s; tax-free meal allowance up to 129.50 CZK/shift (2026)

policies.name: Rodičovský příspěvek (parental allowance)
policies.what: A fixed pot of 350,000 CZK per child (700,000 CZK for multiples) for children born from 1 January 2024, paid monthly at a pace the parent chooses — up to 70% of 30× the daily assessment base (roughly the maternity-benefit level) for insured parents, 13,000 CZK/month max for the uninsured — until the child turns 3. The parent may work; an under-2 may attend nursery up to 92 hours/month without losing it.
policies.value: 700,000 CZK (≈ €28,500) for two children; e.g. ≈ 9,700 CZK/month per child if spread over 3 years, or ≈ 27,000 CZK/month for ~13 months
policies.eligibility: Any parent permanently resident in Czechia caring for the youngest child; no income test, no prior employment needed (only the monthly cap differs).
policies.caveat: Only one allowance per family at a time (for the youngest child), so a second baby ends the first child's unspent balance in effect — draw fast. A rise to 400,000 CZK for children born from 2027 has been reported; verify before relying on it.

policies.name: Peněžitá pomoc v mateřství (maternity benefit) + otcovská (paternity benefit)
policies.what: Sickness-insurance benefit of 70% of the (reduced) daily assessment base for 28 weeks (37 for multiples), starting 6–8 weeks before the due date. From week 7 the father may take the benefit instead of the mother. Separately the father gets 14 days of otcovská at 70% within the first 6 weeks. Both are tax-free.
policies.value: ≈ 27,000 CZK/month (≈ €1,100) for 6.5 months at a median wage (~40,000 CZK gross); father ≈ 12,500 CZK for his 2 weeks
policies.eligibility: 270 days of sickness insurance in the last 2 years (employees are insured automatically); self-employed only if they pay voluntary sickness insurance.
policies.caveat: The daily base is reduced above ~1,550 CZK/day (2026 bands), so replacement falls below 70% for above-average earners.

policies.name: Daňové zvýhodnění na dítě (child tax credit, refundable)
policies.what: Annual income-tax credit of 15,204 CZK for the first child, 22,320 CZK for the second, 27,840 CZK for each further child (2026; double for a ZTP/P child), applied monthly by the employer. If the credit exceeds the tax due, the difference is paid out as a 'daňový bonus'. Claimed by one parent for all children.
policies.value: 37,524 CZK/year (≈ €1,530) for two children — about 3,100 CZK per month
policies.eligibility: A parent with annual earned income of at least 6× the minimum wage (124,800 CZK in 2026); child under 18 (26 if studying) living in the household.
policies.caveat: The separate nursery-fee credit (školkovné, up to ~17,000 CZK/year) was abolished from 2024.

policies.name: Mateřská škola (public kindergarten) — guaranteed place from age 3, low fee
policies.what: Children have a legal right to a place in their catchment public kindergarten from age 3 (from 2 only if capacity allows). The monthly fee is set by the municipality but capped at 8% of the minimum wage — max 1,792 CZK in 2026, typically 500–1,000 CZK — plus meals (~1,000 CZK). The final year before school (age 5–6) is compulsory and free.
policies.value: Full-day public kindergarten for roughly 1,500–2,800 CZK/month (≈ €60–115) per child including meals, free in the last year
policies.eligibility: All children from age 3 with residence in the municipality; priority by age.
policies.caveat: Under-3 care (jesle, dětské skupiny) is scarce and costs roughly 3,000–8,000 CZK/month; big-city kindergartens still turn away 3-year-olds when full despite the entitlement.

policies.name: Sleva na manžela — 24,840 CZK tax credit while the spouse cares for a child under 3
policies.what: The working spouse deducts 24,840 CZK a year from income tax if the other spouse lives in the household, cares for a child under 3 and has own income of at most 68,000 CZK a year (parental allowance does not count; maternity benefit does). Since the 2024 consolidation package the credit exists only in this under-3 situation. Claimed in the annual tax settlement or return, pro rata by month.
policies.value: 24,840 CZK/year (≈ €1,000) for up to about 3 years per child — i.e. while the family draws rodičovský příspěvek; ≈ 2,070 CZK a month on top of the child tax credit
policies.eligibility: Married couples or registered partners in a joint household; spouse's own taxable income ≤ 68,000 CZK/year and youngest child under 3; the claiming spouse needs enough tax (≈ 165,000 CZK taxable income) to use it.
policies.url_label: Finanční správa — dotazy a odpovědi: sleva na manžela
policies.caveat: Unmarried couples get nothing; a part-time job or maternity benefit above 68,000 CZK in the year kills the whole credit (cliff edge); not refundable, unlike the child credit.

policies.name: Statutory right to shorter hours for parents of under-15s (§ 241 ZP) + remote-work request for under-9s
policies.what: A pregnant employee or a parent caring for a child under 15 who asks in writing for shorter working hours (§ 80) or another suitable schedule must be granted it unless serious operational reasons prevent this — a refusal needs written justification (since 2023). Parents of children under 9 may ask for remote work and a refusal must be reasoned in writing (§ 241a). No overtime may be ordered for a parent of a child under 1; after maternity leave the employer must return the employee to the same job and workplace (§ 47). Employers get a 5% social-contribution discount on part-timers caring for a child under 10.
policies.value: e.g. a 30-hour week on request until the youngest child is 15, refusable only for documented operational reasons; guaranteed return to the same job after maternity leave
policies.eligibility: All employees in an employment relationship; no minimum tenure.
policies.caveat: 'Serious operational reasons' is a real escape hatch, especially in small firms; remote work is only a right to a reasoned answer, not to the arrangement itself; return-to-same-job applies after maternity, not after parental leave.

policies.name: 4 weeks paid leave + 13 public holidays; 60% sick pay from day 1; ošetřovné 60% for a sick child
policies.what: Minimum annual leave is 4 weeks (5 in the public sector; many private employers give 5) plus 13 public holidays. Own illness: the employer pays 60% of (reduced) average earnings from the first day for 14 days — the unpaid waiting days were abolished in 2019 — then ČSSZ nemocenské at 60/66/72% for up to 380 days. A sick child under 10: ošetřovné at 60% of the reduced daily base for up to 9 days per illness (16 for single parents), and parents may swap once. Two paid 30-minute breastfeeding breaks per shift until the child is 1.
policies.value: ≈ 6.5 weeks off at full pay per parent (4 weeks + ~9 weekday holidays); a sick week costs roughly 40% of that week's pay
policies.eligibility: All employees; nemocenské and ošetřovné need sickness insurance (automatic for employees with income above 4,500 CZK/month).
policies.caveat: 9 days of ošetřovné per illness is short if both children fall ill in sequence; the employee 0.6% sickness contribution was reintroduced in 2024; the daily base is capped, so 60% is really ≈ 55% for above-average earners.

policies.name: Tax-free meal allowance (stravenky / stravenkový paušál) — up to 129.50 CZK per shift in 2026
policies.what: An employer's contribution to meals — canteen, meal vouchers/cards or a cash 'stravenkový paušál' — is free of income tax and contributions up to 70% of the upper meal-allowance limit for a 5–12 h business trip (185 CZK in 2026 under decree 573/2025), i.e. 129.50 CZK per shift of at least 3 hours worked. It is the most common Czech employee benefit; the state no longer requires an employee co-payment for the cash form.
policies.value: ≈ 30,000 CZK/year (≈ €1,200) per earner untaxed if paid at the limit for ~230 shifts — worth ≈ 45,000 CZK of gross wage; up to twice that for two earners
policies.eligibility: Any employee whose employer offers it (voluntary for private employers, near-standard in mid-size and large firms and the public sector); pro rata for part-time shifts over 3 hours.
policies.url_label: Finanční správa — zaměstnanci a zaměstnavatelé: obecné informace (příspěvek na stravování)
policies.caveat: Not a legal entitlement — small employers often pay less or nothing; amounts above the limit are taxed as wages; other leisure benefits are now capped at half the average wage per year.

policies.name: Superdávka (dávka státní sociální pomoci) — child bonus + rent component
policies.what: From October 2025 the child allowance, housing allowance, subsistence allowance and housing supplement were merged into one means-tested benefit; old benefits stopped in mid-2026. It has four parts: living costs, housing (covers rent above a set share of income), a child bonus (basic ~1,000 CZK per child) and a work bonus. Assessed on household income, assets and work activity.
policies.value: ≈ 2,000 CZK/month child bonus for two kids plus part of the rent — but only while household net income is below roughly 54,000 CZK/month (4× the family's living minimum)
policies.eligibility: Households with dependent children whose net income is under 4× the living minimum and where every adult is work-active (or on parental leave); assets are checked.
policies.caveat: Two full-time median earners are typically just above the line; it becomes reachable when one parent is on parental allowance. New system with long processing times in 2026.

official.label: Úřad práce ČR / MPSV — state social support (family benefits)

guide.label: European Commission — Your social security rights in Czechia

DE.note: Germany combines a solid universal child benefit (€259/child/month in 2026), a well-designed parental allowance (Elterngeld, up to €1,800/month for 12+2 months) and a legal right to a childcare place from age one. The catch is that the right exists on paper: several hundred thousand Kita places are missing, above all in the West, and fees range from zero (Berlin, Rhineland-Palatinate) to several hundred euros a month. Housing benefit (Wohngeld) is not reachable for two median earners, and married-couple tax splitting helps only if the partners' incomes differ a lot. Germany taxes wages heavily (roughly 20% employee social contributions plus income tax) and offers no earned-income credit, but it does index the tariff every two years, charges parents less for long-term-care insurance, protects jobs for three years of Elternzeit with a right to part-time, and lets employers pay Kita fees and a Deutschlandticket entirely tax-free.

headline.cash: €518/month for 2 kids (Kindergeld €259 each, 2026)
headline.leave: Elterngeld 65% of net (max €1,800/month) for 12 + 2 partner months; 14 weeks Mutterschutz at full pay
headline.childcare: legal right to a Kita place from age 1; fees €0 (Berlin) to a few hundred €/month; ~400,000 places missing
headline.tax: 80% of childcare fees deductible up to €4,800/child; Kinderfreibetrag €9,756/child (rarely beats Kindergeld at median)
headline.labourtax: no earned-income credit; brackets shifted +2% and Grundfreibetrag €12,348 for 2026; parents pay 0.25–0.85 pp less Pflegeversicherung than childless colleagues
headline.workrights: 20 days statutory (≈30 typical) + 9–13 holidays; right to 15–32 h part-time during 3-year Elternzeit (firms >15); 6 weeks full sick pay

policies.name: Elterngeld (Basiselterngeld / ElterngeldPlus)
policies.what: Parental allowance replacing 65% of previous net income (67% for low earners), min €300, max €1,800/month, for 12 months, plus 2 partner months if the other parent takes at least 2 months. ElterngeldPlus stretches each month into two at half the rate, usable alongside part-time work. Sibling bonus +10% (min €75) while an older child is under 3.
policies.value: ≈ €1,700/month for ~12–14 months per child at median net pay (≈ €22,000–24,000 per child), plus 10% sibling bonus for the second child
policies.eligibility: Parents living with the child and working at most 32 h/week; taxable household income below €175,000/year (births from April 2025).
policies.caveat: €1,800 cap has not been raised since 2007; Elternzeit (job protection) runs up to 3 years but is unpaid beyond Elterngeld.

policies.name: Kindergeld
policies.what: Universal monthly child benefit of €259 per child (raised from €255 in January 2026), paid by the Familienkasse until age 18 (25 in education), no income test. Low-income families can add Kinderzuschlag (up to roughly €300/child), but two median earners are above its limit.
policies.value: €518/month (€6,216/year) for 2 kids, 2026
policies.eligibility: All parents resident in Germany; one application per child at the Familienkasse.
policies.caveat: Kindergeld is an advance on the child tax allowance; the tax office keeps whichever is better (Günstigerprüfung), so the two do not add up.

policies.name: Legal right to a Kita place from age 1 (§ 24 SGB VIII) + Land fee reductions
policies.what: Every child from its first birthday has an enforceable right to a place in a Kita or with a childminder; the Jugendamt must provide one. Fees are set by Länder and municipalities: Berlin fully free, Hamburg 5 h/day free, Rhineland-Palatinate free from 2, NRW free in the last 2 years, elsewhere income-graded fees.
policies.value: Roughly €0 (Berlin) to €300–€500/month per full-time place for a median family in Bavaria or Baden-Württemberg, more for under-3s; 2 kids can mean €0–€900/month
policies.eligibility: All children from age 1 (from birth if parents work); apply to the municipality, often a year ahead.
policies.caveat: Bertelsmann Stiftung estimates roughly 400,000 places missing (2024/25), mostly in western Länder; opening hours often end mid-afternoon; parents can sue but a court cannot conjure a place.

policies.name: Elternzeit with legal right to part-time (15–32 h/week) + Brückenteilzeit
policies.what: Each parent may take up to 36 months of unpaid, job-protected Elternzeit per child until the 3rd birthday (24 of those months usable until the 8th birthday), with dismissal protection. During Elternzeit a parent in a firm with more than 15 employees and 6 months' tenure can insist on working 15–32 hours a week; silence from the employer counts as consent. Outside Elternzeit, firms with more than 45 staff must grant temporary part-time of 1–5 years (Brückenteilzeit).
policies.value: Up to 3 years of protected job per parent per child, combinable with Elterngeld; a guaranteed 32-hour week for either parent until the child is 3 (or 8 with saved months)
policies.eligibility: All employees living with the child; part-time claim needs >15 employees and 6 months' tenure; Brückenteilzeit needs >45 employees and 6 months' tenure.
policies.caveat: Elternzeit itself is unpaid beyond the 12–14 Elterngeld months; the part-time right does not exist in small firms (≤15 employees), and there is no right to return to full time before the agreed period ends.

policies.name: Mutterschutz + Kinderkrankengeld
policies.what: Maternity protection: 6 weeks before and 8 weeks after birth off work at full net pay (health fund pays €13/day, employer tops up), with dismissal ban. Child-sick leave: each parent may stay home 15 paid days per child per year (max 35 for several children) at 90% of net pay, for children under 12.
policies.value: ≈ 14 weeks of full pay per birth; up to 30 paid days/year per parent for 2 sick kids
policies.eligibility: Employees in statutory health insurance (about 90% of workers); children co-insured free of charge.
policies.caveat: The 15-day Kinderkrankengeld rule is a temporary extension valid to end-2026; from 2027 it may fall back to 10 days unless prolonged.

policies.name: Childcare-cost deduction, Kinderfreibetrag and Ehegattensplitting
policies.what: 80% of paid childcare fees (Kita, childminder) are deductible as special expenses up to €4,800 per child per year (from 2025). The Kinderfreibetrag (€9,756 per child in 2026) is set against Kindergeld and only wins for high earners. Married couples file jointly (splitting), which lowers tax when one partner earns much less, e.g. part-time after a birth.
policies.value: Up to ≈ €1,400 tax saved per child per year on Kita fees at a 30% marginal rate; splitting worth roughly €1,000–3,000/year when one partner goes part-time
policies.eligibility: Anyone filing an income-tax return; splitting requires marriage or registered partnership.
policies.caveat: Unmarried couples get no splitting; the childcare deduction is worthless in Länder where Kita is already free.

policies.name: Paid leave, full sick pay and tax-free Kita subsidy / Deutschlandticket from the employer
policies.what: Statutory minimum leave is 24 working days (20 days on a 5-day week); collective agreements typically give 30, plus 9 nationwide public holidays (up to 13 in Bavaria). Employers pay 100% salary for the first 6 weeks of each illness (§ 3 EFZG), then health insurance pays 70% for up to 78 weeks. Employers can add, free of tax and contributions and without limit, contributions to Kita or childminder fees for pre-school children (§ 3 Nr. 33 EStG), a job ticket/Deutschlandticket (§ 3 Nr. 15 EStG, ≈ €63/month in 2026) and €50/month in benefits in kind.
policies.value: ≈ 39 paid days off per year per parent; an employer Kita subsidy of e.g. €300/month per child is worth roughly €5,000/year net for 2 kids because no tax or contributions are due
policies.eligibility: All employees (leave, sick pay after 4 weeks' employment); employer extras are voluntary and must be paid on top of the agreed salary.
policies.caveat: The Kita subsidy and job ticket exist only if the employer offers them; in Länder with free Kita there is nothing to subsidise. 20 days' statutory leave is among the lowest in Western Europe; the 30 days are a collective-agreement norm, not law.

policies.name: Lower Pflegeversicherung contributions for parents (Kinderabschlag)
policies.what: Long-term-care insurance costs 3.6% of gross pay (employee share 1.8%) since 2025. Childless employees over 23 pay a 0.6-point surcharge; parents pay no surcharge and get a further 0.25-point reduction per child from the 2nd to the 5th child while the child is under 25 (since July 2023, after a Constitutional Court ruling).
policies.value: With 2 kids each earner pays 1.55% instead of 1.8% (childless: 2.4%): about €120/year less per earner at a €48,000 median wage, and roughly €400/year less than a childless colleague; ≈ €250–800 per household per year
policies.eligibility: All employees in statutory long-term-care insurance with children under 25; the employer applies the discount once parenthood is proven (birth certificate).
policies.caveat: The first child only removes the childless surcharge; the reduction ends when the child turns 25; the overall rate has risen twice since 2023 and further increases are being debated for 2027.

policies.name: Tariff indexation against fiscal drag (2025/2026) and the 2027 income-tax reform
policies.what: The Steuerfortentwicklungsgesetz raised the tax-free Grundfreibetrag to €12,096 (2025) and €12,348 (2026) and shifted all brackets by 2.6% and 2.0% to offset inflation; the top rate now starts at €69,878. A cabinet draft of 2 September 2026 goes further: Grundfreibetrag €12,564 (2027) and €12,900 (2028), a flatter second bracket up to €70,600, Arbeitnehmer-Pauschbetrag €1,430, Kindergeld €267/€272.
policies.value: The 2026 shift is worth roughly €100–150 per earner compared with frozen brackets; the government says a median-income family with 2 children gains more than €600/year from 2028 (including higher Kindergeld)
policies.eligibility: All income-tax payers; applied automatically in payroll.
policies.caveat: Germany has no automatic indexation; each adjustment needs a law and the 2027/2028 reform is still a draft. Employee social contributions (≈ 21% of gross in 2026) are not indexed and keep rising.

official.label: Familienportal des Bundes (all federal family benefits)

guide.label: EU Your Europe — Family benefits

DK.note: Denmark delivers most of its family support in kind: a guaranteed, heavily subsidised crèche place from 26 weeks, free healthcare and child dental care, and 24 weeks of paid leave per parent (often topped up to full pay by collective agreements). Cash is modest and there is no family tax splitting; the income-tested childcare and housing benefits are out of reach for two median earners, and Copenhagen rents are high. From 1 January 2027 the parent share of childcare cost falls from 25% to 21.3%. Wage taxation is heavy (8% AM-bidrag plus ≈ 37% on the rest at median wage), softened by an employment deduction worth ≈ 16,600 kr per earner; beyond the statutory 5 weeks of holiday, most everyday parent rights (paid sick-child days, a 6th holiday week, full pay when ill) come from collective agreements rather than law.

headline.cash: ≈ 3,580 kr/month (≈ €480) tax-free for two children under 3 (børne- og ungeydelse, 2026)
headline.leave: 24 weeks paid leave per parent after birth (48 shared) + 4 weeks before; state benefit max 5,085 kr/week, employers often top up to full pay
headline.childcare: guaranteed place from 26 weeks; parents pay max 25% of cost (21.3% from 2027) — Copenhagen crèche 3,555 kr/month, 50% sibling discount
headline.tax: no family tax splitting or child tax credit; only the transferable personal allowance between spouses
headline.labourtax: beskæftigelsesfradrag 12.75% of wage (max 63,300 kr, 2026) + jobfradrag: ≈ 16,600 kr tax saved per earner; brackets wage-indexed yearly
headline.workrights: 5 weeks paid leave (25 days) + ≈ 10 public holidays; 5 unpaid care days/yr since 2023; right to request flexible work until child is 9

policies.name: Dagtilbud: pasningsgaranti + fee cap + søskendetilskud
policies.what: Municipalities must offer a childcare place from age 26 weeks (pasningsgaranti). Parents pay at most 25% of the gross operating cost (21.3% from 1 Jan 2027); the state/municipality covers the rest. Copenhagen 2026: crèche (0–2 y) 3,555 kr/month, kindergarten (3–5 y) 1,988 kr, lunch extra. 50% sibling discount on the cheaper place.
policies.value: ≈ 5,300 kr/month (≈ €715) for two crèche places in Copenhagen; the subsidy is worth ≈ 10,600 kr/month per place
policies.eligibility: All resident children; income-tested free places (fripladstilskud) only below 677,500 kr household income (2026), i.e. not at two median wages.
policies.caveat: Fees vary by municipality (crèche typically 3,300–4,500 kr/month in 2026); places may be offered far from home; staffing ratios (minimumsnormeringer) still uneven.

policies.name: Barselsorlov + barselsdagpenge
policies.what: Since Aug 2022 each parent gets 24 weeks of paid leave after birth (mother also 4 weeks before). For employees 11 weeks per parent are earmarked (2 right after birth + 9 non-transferable); 13 weeks each are transferable. Barselsdagpenge is max 5,085 kr/week in 2026 (≈ 22,000 kr/month); most collective agreements top up to full salary for much of it.
policies.value: 48 weeks shared paid leave; ≈ 22,000 kr/month (≈ €2,950) from the state ≈ 47% of a 47,000 kr median wage, often 100% with employer top-up
policies.eligibility: Employees with 160 hours in the 4 months before leave (also self-employed/unemployed with other rules).
policies.caveat: Without a collective agreement the state rate is a big pay cut at median wage; earmarked weeks not used by a parent are lost.

policies.name: Børne- og ungeydelse (child and youth benefit)
policies.what: Universal, tax-free, paid quarterly by Udbetaling Danmark and split between the parents. 2026 rates: 5,370 kr/quarter per child aged 0–2, 4,251 kr for 3–6 (lower for 7–17). Reduced by 2% of each parent's own income above 961,100 kr (2026), so untouched at median wages.
policies.value: ≈ 3,580 kr/month (≈ €480) for a newborn + toddler; ≈ 3,200 kr once one child turns 3
policies.eligibility: Residents with children under 18; full rate after 6 years' residence/work in DK/EEA (phased in otherwise).

policies.name: Beskæftigelsesfradrag + jobfradrag (employment and job deductions)
policies.what: Automatic deduction of 12.75% of wage income (2026 rate, up from 10.65% in 2023 under the 2023 personal-tax reform), capped at 63,300 kr, plus a jobfradrag of 4.5% of income above 235,200 kr (max 3,100 kr). Both are 'ligningsmæssige fradrag' worth the municipal + church tax rate (≈ 25%). Thresholds are regulated every year by personskattelovens § 20.
policies.value: ≈ 16,600 kr (≈ €2,220) less tax per earner at a 47,000 kr monthly wage (cap reached), ≈ 33,000 kr (≈ €4,450) per household per year
policies.eligibility: Everyone with wage or self-employment income; applied automatically on the forskudsopgørelse.
policies.caveat: It only offsets part of a high wage tax: 8% AM-bidrag, 12.01% bundskat and ≈ 25% kommuneskat still apply; the extra 11.5% deduction is for single parents only.

policies.name: Ferieloven: 5 weeks paid holiday + ferietillæg
policies.what: Every employee earns 2.08 paid holiday days per month = 25 days (5 weeks) a year, taken concurrently (accrual Sept–Aug, use Sept–Dec of the following year); 3 consecutive weeks may be taken May–Sept. Salaried staff get pay plus a 1% ferietillæg, hourly staff 12.5% feriegodtgørelse. Most collective agreements add 5 'feriefridage' (a 6th week). ≈ 10 public holidays on top.
policies.value: 25 paid days (+ 5 under most agreements) + ≈ 10 public holidays ≈ 7 weeks off per parent per year at full pay
policies.eligibility: All employees from the first month of employment; holidays accrue with pay from day one.
policies.caveat: The 6th week and the 1–3% holiday bonus above the statutory 1% depend on the collective agreement; Store Bededag was abolished as a public holiday in 2024.

policies.name: Omsorgsorlov (5 care days) + right to request flexible working (EU work-life-balance rules)
policies.what: Under the 2022 transposition of the EU work-life-balance directive every employee has 5 care days (omsorgsorlov) per calendar year from 1 January 2023 to look after a seriously ill child/partner/parent, and parents of children under 9 (and carers) may request flexible working arrangements (reduced or shifted hours, remote work); the employer must answer within a reasonable time and justify a refusal. Dismissal for using these rights is banned.
policies.value: 5 protected care days per parent per year + a formal route to part-time/remote work until the youngest is 9; paid 'barns 1. og 2. sygedag' in most collective agreements
policies.eligibility: All employees; the flexible-working request requires 6 months' seniority; care days need a doctor's note if the employer asks.
policies.caveat: Both are unpaid by law: the 5 care days are 'selvbetalt' and the employer may refuse flexible working with reasons (the request right is in the same act but not detailed on the linked page); paid sick-child days exist only via collective agreements (typically the child's first and second sick day).

policies.name: Omsorgsorlov + right to request flexible working (EU work-life-balance rules since 2 Aug 2022)
policies.what: Since 2 August 2022 every employee has 5 care days (omsorgsorlov) per calendar year to look after a seriously ill child/partner/parent, and parents of children under 9 (and carers) may request flexible working arrangements (reduced or shifted hours, remote work); the employer must answer within a reasonable time and give reasons for a refusal. Job protection and a ban on dismissal for using these rights apply.
policies.value: 5 protected care days per parent per year + a formal route to part-time/remote work until the youngest is 9; paid 'barns 1. og 2. sygedag' in most collective agreements
policies.eligibility: All employees; the flexible-working request requires 6 months' seniority; care days need a doctor's note if the employer asks.
policies.caveat: Both are unpaid by law: the 5 care days are 'selvbetalt' and the employer may refuse flexible working with reasons; paid sick-child days exist only via collective agreements (typically the child's first and second sick day).

policies.name: Free child healthcare, health visitor and dental care
policies.what: GP, hospital and 7 free preventive child examinations (age 0–5) plus vaccinations are free. A municipal health visitor (sundhedsplejerske) makes home visits in the baby's first year. Municipal dental care is free for children and young people up to age 22 (extension to 18–21-year-olds phased in 2022–2025). Public school (folkeskole) is free.
policies.value: ≈ 0 kr out of pocket for child health and dental care
policies.eligibility: All residents with a Danish health card (sundhedskort).
policies.caveat: Adult dental care is not free; school lunch is not provided free nationally.
