IE.note: Ireland's support for a working couple is universal but thin: €140/month per child, flat-rate €299/week leave that replaces less than half a median wage, and a childcare subsidy that at two median incomes falls back to the universal €2.14/hour, leaving full-time crèche bills of roughly €180-200/week per child even under the fee cap. The strong points are free pre-school (ECCE) for two years from age 2 years 8 months, free GP care under 8, free primary schoolbooks and hot school meals, and generous employer-independent leave weeks. Rent is the biggest unaddressed cost: housing supports (HAP) are not available at this income; only the €1,000 renter tax credit and the Help to Buy scheme for a first new-build home apply. Labour taxes are low at a median wage because €4,000 of credits per earner wipe out tax on the first €20,000 and the dual-earner 20% band reaches €88,000, but the work-rights side is thin: sick pay is 5 days, flexible working is only a right to ask, and non-cash perks (vouchers, TaxSaver, bike scheme) depend on the employer.

headline.cash: €280/month for 2 kids (Child Benefit €140/child, unchanged in Budget 2026)
headline.leave: 26 weeks maternity + 2 weeks paternity + 9 weeks per parent, all at a flat €299/week (2026)
headline.childcare: NCS universal subsidy €2.14/hour (≈ €96/week/child); income-assessed up to €5.10/hour below €68k net income; fee cap €295/week
headline.healthedu: ECCE: 15 hours/week free pre-school for 2 years; free GP visits under 8; free primary schoolbooks and hot school meals
headline.labourtax: Employee Tax Credit €2,000 + Personal Credit €2,000 per earner (unchanged 2026); 20% band €53,000 + €35,000 for dual earners; USC 2% band widened to €28,700
headline.workrights: 4 weeks leave + 10 holidays; statutory sick pay only 5 days at 70% (max €110); right to request (not have) flexible work for parents of under-12s; €1,500 tax-free vouchers

policies.name: National Childcare Scheme (NCS) + core-funding fee cap
policies.what: Government pays part of the crèche bill directly to the provider. Universal subsidy (no means test): €2.14/hour for up to 45 hours/week per child. Income-assessed subsidy from 31 Aug 2026: up to €5.10/hour at net family income ≤ €34,000, tapering to zero at €68,000, after a €5,500 discount for 2 children. Core-funded services must cap fees at €295/week (2025-26).
policies.value: ≈ €96/week per child (≈ €830/month for 2 in full-time care) at two median wages; parents still pay ≈ €180-200/week per child
policies.eligibility: Children 24 weeks to 15 years in a Tusla-registered, NCS-contracted service; 45 subsidised hours need both parents working/studying.
policies.caveat: At two median wages net income sits at or above the €68,000 cut-off, so only the universal rate applies. Places are scarce (waiting lists from pregnancy in Dublin) and Irish fees remain among the EU's highest. A lower fee cap (about €280/week for 45 hours) was announced for services from September 2026.

policies.name: Employee (PAYE) Tax Credit + Personal Tax Credit and the dual-earner standard-rate band
policies.what: Each employee gets a €2,000 Employee Tax Credit (capped at 20% of PAYE income below €10,000) plus a €2,000 Personal Tax Credit, both left unchanged in Budget 2026. A married/civil-partner couple with two incomes pays 20% on up to €53,000 for one earner plus the lower earner's income up to €35,000 (max €88,000 combined) before the 40% rate. Budget 2026 widened the 2% USC band to €28,700.
policies.value: ≈ €4,000/year per earner (≈ €8,000 for the couple) off income tax; at two ≈ €45,000 wages all income stays in the 20% band, so net tax ≈ €5,000 each
policies.eligibility: Automatic through PAYE for anyone with PAYE income; credits granted via Revenue myAccount tax credit certificate.
policies.url_label: Revenue — Tax rates, bands and reliefs (2026 chart)
policies.caveat: Credits and bands were frozen in Budget 2026 (no indexation, so wage rises push more income into the 40% band); PRSI rises to 4.3% in Oct 2026 and USC still takes 3% on income between €28,700 and €70,044.

policies.name: Maternity Benefit, Paternity Benefit and Parent's Benefit
policies.what: Maternity leave: 26 weeks with Maternity Benefit of €299/week (from Jan 2026) plus 16 unpaid weeks. Paternity leave: 2 weeks at €299/week. Parent's leave: 9 weeks per parent, non-transferable, in the child's first 2 years, at €299/week. All paid by the Department of Social Protection on PRSI record; employers may top up but need not.
policies.value: ≈ €13,150 per birth from the state (26 + 2 + 9 + 9 weeks x €299) — under half of a median wage while on leave
policies.eligibility: Employees and self-employed with 39+ PRSI weeks in the relevant period; leave itself is a statutory right for all employees.
policies.caveat: Flat rate, not earnings-related: a median earner (~€45,000) loses roughly half of net pay each week on leave unless the employer tops up, which many small employers do not.

policies.name: Child Benefit
policies.what: Universal monthly payment of €140 per child, paid on the first Tuesday of the month to the parent, tax-free and not means-tested, until 16 (or 19 in education). Rate was not changed in Budget 2026; a means-tested second tier for low-income families is planned but not yet introduced.
policies.value: €280/month (€3,360/year) for 2 children
policies.eligibility: All children ordinarily resident in Ireland; automatic registration at birth for Irish-born children.
policies.caveat: Frozen at €140 since 2016 apart from one-off double payments; real value has eroded. The Child Support Payment increases in Budget 2026 apply only to families on welfare payments.

policies.name: Annual leave, public holidays, statutory sick pay, force majeure and breastfeeding breaks, right to request flexible working
policies.what: 4 working weeks' paid leave plus 10 public holidays (St Brigid's Day added 2023). Statutory sick pay: 5 days/year at 70% of pay up to €110/day after 13 weeks' service (planned rise to 7 days deferred). Force majeure leave: 3 paid days in 12 months (5 in 36) for a sick child. Breastfeeding breaks: 1 paid hour/day until the child is 2. Since March 2024 parents of under-12s can request flexible working after 6 months' service; the employer must answer within 4 weeks.
policies.value: ≈ 30 paid days off/year per earner + 3 paid sick-child days + ≈ €380/week sick pay for 5 days; flexible working is a request only
policies.eligibility: All employees; sick pay after 13 weeks' service; flexible-working request after 6 months' service; parental leave (26 weeks per child under 12) is unpaid.
policies.url_label: Workplace Relations Commission — Sick leave (statutory sick pay)
policies.caveat: Sick pay beyond 5 days depends on the employer or Illness Benefit (€244/week from day 4); flexible-working requests can be refused on business grounds and the WRC only reviews the process, not the merits; parental leave is entirely unpaid.

policies.name: Tax-free in-kind perks: Small Benefit Exemption, TaxSaver commuter ticket, Cycle to Work, remote-working relief
policies.what: Employers can give up to 5 non-cash benefits (vouchers) a year worth €1,500 in total, free of tax, PRSI and USC (from 1 Jan 2025). TaxSaver: an annual public-transport pass bought by the employer or via salary sacrifice is exempt from BIK. Cycle to Work: a bike up to €1,250 (€1,500 e-bike, €3,000 cargo) every 4 years via salary sacrifice. Remote workers can claim 30% of electricity, heating and broadband for days worked at home, or a tax-free €3.20/day from the employer.
policies.value: up to ≈ €1,500/year in vouchers per earner tax-free (worth ≈ €2,800 gross at 48.5%) + ≈ 48.5% off a commuter pass or bike if the employer runs the schemes; remote relief ≈ €100-200/year
policies.eligibility: At the employer's discretion (voucher scheme widely used, especially at Christmas); remote-working relief claimed by the employee on the tax return.
policies.caveat: None of these is a legal entitlement; vouchers cannot be exchanged for cash and unused allowance does not carry forward; the bike-to-work and TaxSaver savings only apply at the 40%/marginal rate if the employer operates salary sacrifice.

policies.name: ECCE free pre-school + free GP care under 8 + free primary schoolbooks and hot school meals
policies.what: ECCE: 3 hours/day, 5 days/week, 38 weeks/year of free pre-school for 2 years, from the September after a child turns 2 years 8 months. GP visit card: free GP visits and assessments for every child under 8, no means test. Primary school: free schoolbooks and workbooks (since 2023) and hot school meals in all primary schools eligible from 2025.
policies.value: ≈ €70/week per child in ECCE (state pays the provider) + ≈ €60-70 per avoided GP visit + ≈ €100-150/year books/meals per primary pupil
policies.eligibility: Universal for resident children; ECCE via any participating pre-school; GP card via HSE registration.
policies.caveat: ECCE covers only 15 hours/week in term time; working parents still pay for wrap-around hours (NCS-subsidised). Free GP care ends at 8; prescriptions and hospital A&E charges still apply.

guide.label: Citizens Information — Budget 2026 (family, childcare, housing)

IS.note: Iceland pays 12 months of parental leave at 80% of wages (cap raised to 900,000 ISK/month in 2026) and, in Reykjavík, preschool is now free for the first 36 hours a week. The famous weakness is the 'care gap': municipal preschool places usually start around 18 months, six months after leave ends, and rents are very high. The income-tested child benefit (barnabætur) is largely phased out at two median wages and the housing benefit is out of reach for them; there is no family taxation. Iceland's 31.49% first tax bracket bites from the first króna, but the annually indexed personal tax credit (≈ 870,000 ISK per earner in 2026) and near-universal collective-agreement rights — 12 paid sick-child days per parent, full-pay sick leave, holiday and December bonuses — do a lot of the work that statute does elsewhere.

headline.cash: ≈ 340,000 ISK/year (≈ €2,350) barnabætur for 2 children at two median wages — the under-7 supplement is fully phased out
headline.leave: 12 months total (6 per parent, 6 weeks transferable) at 80% of wage, max 900,000 ISK/month (2026)
headline.childcare: Reykjavík: first 36 h/week free since April 2026; 8 h/day ≈ 33,300 ISK/month incl. meals — but places typically only from ≈ 18 months
headline.tax: none: only the personal tax credit is transferable between spouses
headline.labourtax: persónuafsláttur 72,492 ISK/month (2026) = ≈ 870,000 ISK (≈ €5,900) less tax per earner, unused part transferable to spouse; brackets indexed yearly
headline.workrights: 24 statutory holiday days (25–30 by agreement) + ≈ 12 public holidays; 12 paid sick-child days/yr per parent; 4 months' unpaid parental leave per child until 8

policies.name: Fæðingarorlof (parental leave from the Maternity/Paternity Leave Fund)
policies.what: 12 months of paid leave per birth: 6 months for each parent, of which up to 6 weeks can be transferred to the other. Payment is 80% of average total earnings, capped at 900,000 ISK/month for leave taken from 1 Jan 2026 (800,000 in 2025); minimum 275,688 ISK for 50–100% jobs. Must be used before the child turns 2.
policies.value: ≈ 680,000 ISK/month (≈ €4,700) at an 850,000 ISK median wage, for 6 months each parent
policies.eligibility: Worked continuously in Iceland for 6 months before the birth at ≥ 25%; others get a flat parental grant (fæðingarstyrkur).
policies.caveat: Cap means higher earners lose more; the 6 weeks transferable are lost if the other parent does not use their months.

policies.name: Leikskóli (municipal preschool) — Reykjavík fee schedule
policies.what: Reykjavík (≈ 1/3 of the population; other municipalities similar) charges no tuition for the first 36 h/week since 1 April 2026; an 8-hour day costs 18,000 ISK tuition + 15,290 ISK meals ≈ 33,300 ISK/month, with 20–40% discounts below 18 / 11 million ISK household income; older siblings pay no tuition. Places are ranked by age, mostly from ≈ 18 months.
policies.value: ≈ 33,300 ISK/month (≈ €230) for a full 8-hour place incl. meals for the toddler; the baby will likely wait until ≈ 18 months
policies.eligibility: Children registered in Reykjavík, waiting list from 6 months; earliest start 12 months for priority cases.
policies.caveat: The gap between 12-month leave and an 18–24-month place must be bridged with subsidised childminders (dagforeldrar, often 100,000+ ISK/month net) or unpaid time; staff shortages cause closures.

policies.name: Persónuafsláttur (personal tax credit) with annual indexation and spouse transfer
policies.what: A credit of 72,492 ISK per month in 2026 (68,691 ISK in 2025) set against the 31.49% first-bracket tax (state + municipal) that applies to the first 498,122 ISK/month; unused monthly credit accumulates within the year and up to 100% of an unused credit can be transferred to a spouse. Credit and bracket thresholds are indexed every January to inflation (plus a productivity uplift since 2020).
policies.value: ≈ 870,000 ISK (≈ €5,900) less tax per earner per year, ≈ 1.74 million ISK (≈ €11,800) per household, fully used at an 850,000 ISK monthly wage
policies.eligibility: All residents aged 16+ with taxable income; applied through the employer's withholding.
policies.caveat: A universal credit rather than a work-specific one; the 4% mandatory pension contribution and the second bracket (37.99% above 498,122 ISK/month) still apply, and the credit does not carry over between years.

policies.name: Barnabætur (income-tested child benefit)
policies.what: Paid via the tax system in four instalments. 2026: 345,000 ISK per child per year for couples (514,500 for single parents) plus 130,000 ISK per child under 7. Reduced by 4% of the couple's joint income above 11,688,000 ISK/year; the under-7 supplement is reduced separately by 4% per child, so it disappears quickly.
policies.value: ≈ 340,000 ISK/year (≈ €2,350, ≈ 28,000 ISK/month) for two children at ≈ 20.4 million ISK joint income; zero above ≈ 29 million ISK
policies.eligibility: Tax-resident parents of children under 18; assessed on the previous year's tax return.
policies.caveat: Heavily income-tested: worth much more to below-median households; amounts unchanged from 2025 in nominal terms.

policies.name: Veikindi barna (paid sick-child days) + foreldraorlof (unpaid parental leave until 8)
policies.what: Collective agreements (VR, SGS and the public sector) give each parent 12 paid days per 12 months to care for a sick child under 13 (2 days per month worked in the first 6 months), at full pay incl. shift supplements. By statute (Act 144/2020, arts 44–49) each parent also has a non-transferable right to 4 months' unpaid foreldraorlof per child until the child turns 8, in flexible blocks or as reduced hours by agreement, with a guaranteed return to the same or equivalent job.
policies.value: 24 paid sick-child days per year for the couple (≈ 1 month of salary protected) + 8 months of job-protected unpaid leave per child
policies.eligibility: Sick-child days: all employees covered by a collective agreement (nearly all); foreldraorlof: 6 months' service, 6 weeks' notice.
policies.caveat: The 12 sick-child days come from collective agreements, not from the law; foreldraorlof is unpaid and there is no statutory right to reduced hours, only an obligation on the employer to try to accommodate requests (art. 45).

policies.name: Orlof (annual leave) + full-pay sick leave under Act 30/1987 and collective agreements
policies.what: Orlofslög 30/1987: 2 days per month worked = 24 days (10.17% orlofslaun), main leave 2 May–15 Sept; collective agreements raise this to 25–30 days with seniority and add a holiday bonus (orlofsuppbót) and a December bonus (desemberuppbót), roughly 60,000 and 115,000 ISK in 2025 under the VR/SGS agreements. Own illness: 2 days' full pay per month worked in the first year, then 2 months per 12 months after 1 year (4 months after 5 years). ≈ 12 public holidays plus 2 half-days.
policies.value: 24–30 paid days + ≈ 12 holidays per parent, ≈ 175,000 ISK (≈ €1,200) of bonuses per earner, and full pay for at least 2 months of illness a year after one year in the job
policies.eligibility: All employees; bonus amounts and sick-pay escalation per the applicable collective agreement.
policies.caveat: The statutory floor is only 24 days; the extra days, bonuses and long sick-pay entitlements are collective-agreement terms.

policies.name: Free child healthcare, well-baby care and dental care
policies.what: Children under 2 pay nothing for public healthcare; from 2 to 18 care is free at the health centre and with a referral, otherwise a monthly out-of-pocket cap of 25,198 ISK applies (2026). Well-baby clinic check-ups and vaccinations are free. Children's dental care is fully covered except one 2,500 ISK annual fee (register with a family dentist).
policies.value: ≈ 0–2,500 ISK/year out of pocket for child health and dental
policies.eligibility: All children insured in Iceland (6 months' residence).
policies.caveat: Orthodontics is only partly subsidised; GP appointments in the capital area can take weeks.

IT.note: Italy's support is cash-heavy and ISEE-tested: the Assegno Unico is paid to every family but its size depends on the ISEE indicator, which for a renting two-earner couple with two small children usually lands in the middle-to-upper band. Nursery costs are cushioned by the Bonus Nido (up to €3,600/yr) but public nido places cover only about a third of under-3s and far fewer in the South. Leave is decent for mothers (5 months at 80%) but paternity is 10 days and most shared parental leave is paid at 30%; preschool from 3 is free. On the wage side Italy is generous in small pieces — a permanent €1,000 cuneo deduction per median earner, a 33% middle rate from 2026, tax-free meal vouchers and €2,000 of fringe benefits for parents, two paid hours a day for nursing — but employee contributions of 9.19% and no legal right to part-time mean the household still relies on the ISEE-tested cash rather than on cheaper work.

headline.cash: Assegno Unico ≈ €400–580/month for a newborn + toddler at ISEE €15–25k (2026), min ≈ €120/month above ISEE €46.6k; €1,000 birth bonus
headline.leave: 5 months maternity at 80% + 10 days paternity at 100%; 3 shared months at 80% (rest of 10–11 months at 30%)
headline.childcare: Bonus Nido up to €3,600/yr per child under 3 (ISEE ≤ €40k); free state scuola dell'infanzia 3–6, but nido places scarce
headline.tax: no child tax credit for under-21s since 2022 (folded into Assegno Unico); working mothers of 2+ get €60/month bonus mamme
headline.labourtax: taglio del cuneo: €1,000/yr extra deduction at €20–32k (tax-free bonus up to 7.1% below €20k); IRPEF 28–50k rate cut 35%→33% in 2026
headline.workrights: 4 weeks leave + 12 holidays; 2 h/day paid nursing breaks until age 1; €10/day tax-free meal vouchers and €2,000 fringe benefits for parents

policies.name: Assegno Unico e Universale (AUU)
policies.what: Monthly benefit per child from the 7th month of pregnancy to 21 (no limit for disabled). 2026: €203.80 per child at ISEE ≤ €17,468.51, tapering to €58.30 at ISEE ≥ €46,582.71 or without ISEE. Add-ons: +50% for each child under 1; up to +€34.90 per child when both parents work; +€34.90 for 3+ children. Tax-free, paid by INPS.
policies.value: roughly €400–580/month for a newborn + toddler at ISEE €15–25k (typical for renting two-earner families); ≈ €120/month with no ISEE
policies.eligibility: Residents (EU citizens or 2-year residence permit), Italian tax residence; apply once to INPS, renew ISEE each year by 28 Feb.
policies.url_label: INPS — Assegno unico e universale per i figli a carico
policies.caveat: ISEE counts income AND assets (20%) with a rent deduction up to ~€7,000, so savings or a modest inheritance shrink the benefit; without a valid ISEE you get the minimum only.

policies.name: Bonus asilo nido + free scuola dell'infanzia 3–6
policies.what: INPS reimburses nursery fees (public or licensed private) for children under 3: up to €3,600/yr (11 monthly instalments) for children born from 2024 with ISEE ≤ €40,000; €1,500/yr above €40,000 or without ISEE. From 2026 one application lasts until the child turns 3. From age 3 state scuola dell'infanzia is free (meals charged, income-scaled).
policies.value: ≈ €300/month per child in nursery (up to €7,200/yr for two under-3s); then ≈ €4,000–6,000/yr saved per child from 3 in a free state preschool
policies.eligibility: Child under 3 enrolled in a nido; parent applies online to INPS with receipts; ISEE minorenni.
policies.caveat: Bonus cannot exceed fees actually paid and is paid in arrears; public nido coverage is ~30% of under-3s nationally (under 15% in parts of the South), so many families pay €400–700/month privately and wait for the refund.

policies.name: Taglio del cuneo fiscale (L. 207/2024, permanent from 2025) + IRPEF 33% middle rate (2026)
policies.what: Employees with income up to €20,000 get a tax-free bonus of 7.1% (≤ €8,500), 5.3% (≤ €15,000) or 4.8% (≤ €20,000) of wages; from €20,000 to €32,000 an extra €1,000/yr IRPEF deduction, tapering to zero at €40,000. From 2026 the €28,001–50,000 bracket is taxed at 33% instead of 35% (up to €440/yr). Paid monthly via the employer.
policies.value: ≈ €1,000/yr per earner at €22,000–32,000 (≈ €2,000/household), plus up to €440 each for the part of pay above €28,000
policies.eligibility: Employees (not self-employed) with total income ≤ €40,000; the employer applies it automatically, adjusted in the annual return.
policies.url_label: Agenzia delle Entrate — Circolare 4/E 2025 on the employee bonus and extra deduction (PDF)
policies.caveat: The €1,000 deduction replaces the earlier 6–7% contribution cut and is worth less than it for wages around €30,000; the bonus tapers steeply between €32,000 and €40,000, an implicit 12.5% marginal rate on raises.

policies.name: Congedo di maternità, paternità obbligatorio e congedo parentale
policies.what: Mother: 5 months compulsory maternity leave at 80% of pay (many collective agreements top up to 100%). Father: 10 working days at 100%. Then up to 10 shared months of parental leave (11 if the father takes 3+), usable to age 14: since 2025 three of the couple's months are paid at 80% if taken before age 6, rest 30%.
policies.value: ≈ 5.5 months of near-full pay for the mother per birth + 3 months at 80% shared; further months cost 70% of one salary
policies.eligibility: Employees registered with INPS (self-employed and gig workers have reduced versions).
policies.url_label: INPS — Indennità di congedo parentale per lavoratori dipendenti
policies.caveat: The 80% months are shared between parents, not per parent; parental leave at 30% is rarely affordable, so fathers take little of it.

policies.name: Riposi giornalieri (nursing breaks), sick-child leave, smart-working priority and statutory leave
policies.what: One parent gets 2 paid hours a day (1 if the day is under 6 h) until the child's first birthday, paid 100% by INPS. Unlimited unpaid job-protected leave for a sick child under 3 (5 days/yr each at 3–8). Under-12 parents get priority for smart working and part-time; 4 weeks leave + 12 holidays.
policies.value: ≈ 25% of working time paid but not worked for ≈ 7 months per child (≈ €4,000–5,000 of paid time at a median wage); 20 working days + 12 holidays per earner
policies.eligibility: Employees registered with INPS; riposi are alternative between parents (the father can use them if the mother works or is self-employed).
policies.url_label: INPS — Indennità per riposi giornalieri per padri e madri dipendenti
policies.caveat: There is no legal RIGHT to part-time or remote work for parents in Italy, only priority when the employer offers it; sick-child leave under 3 is unpaid, so it is used sparingly.

policies.name: Buoni pasto (tax-free meal vouchers) and €2,000 fringe-benefit allowance for parents
policies.what: Electronic meal vouchers are exempt from tax and contributions up to €10 per working day from 1 Jan 2026 (was €8; paper €4). Employees with dependent children may also receive up to €2,000/yr of tax-free fringe benefits in 2025–2027 (€1,000 for others), including reimbursement of rent, electricity, gas and water bills. Common in medium and large firms and collective agreements.
policies.value: ≈ €2,200/yr of tax-free vouchers per earner (220 days × €10) plus up to €2,000 of untaxed rent/utility reimbursements per parent — roughly €1,200–1,800/yr in tax and contributions saved per earner where offered
policies.eligibility: Employees whose employer or collective agreement provides vouchers/welfare; the €2,000 limit requires declaring the dependent children's tax codes to the employer.
policies.url_label: Agenzia delle Entrate — Circolari 2025 (Legge di Bilancio 2025/2026 employee measures)
policies.caveat: Nothing obliges an employer to offer vouchers or welfare; small firms and much of the South rarely do, and exceeding the fringe threshold makes the whole amount taxable.

policies.name: Flat 15% tax on night/holiday/shift allowances and 5% on productivity bonuses (2026)
policies.what: For 2026 the Budget Law taxes night-work, Sunday/holiday and shift allowances at a 15% substitute tax (instead of IRPEF plus surcharges) up to €1,500/yr for employees with income ≤ €40,000. Performance bonuses under company agreements are taxed at 5% up to €3,000 (2025–2027), and pay rises from collective agreements signed 2024–2026 at 5% for income ≤ €33,000.
policies.value: ≈ €150–300/yr saved per earner who works shifts or gets a company performance bonus; zero for a standard day job without a premium
policies.eligibility: Employees with income ≤ €40,000 (allowances) or ≤ €80,000 (productivity bonus, needs a registered company/territorial agreement); applied by the employer.
policies.url_label: Agenzia delle Entrate — Comunicato stampa 24 Feb 2026 (imposta sostitutiva 15% and 5%)
policies.caveat: Temporary (2026 only for the 15% rate) and worth little for parents of small children who avoid night and shift work; productivity bonuses exist mainly in unionised large firms.

policies.name: Bonus nuovi nati (€1,000 birth bonus) + Bonus mamme lavoratrici
policies.what: One-off €1,000 from INPS for every child born or adopted from 1 Jan 2025 in families with ISEE ≤ €40,000 (confirmed for 2026). Separately, employed mothers with at least 2 children and income ≤ €40,000 get a tax-free 'bonus mamme' of €60/month (€720/yr) in 2026, until the younger child turns 10.
policies.value: ≈ €1,000 per birth + €720/yr for the mother while she has two children under 10
policies.eligibility: ISEE ≤ €40,000 (nuovi nati); employed/self-employed mothers of 2+ children with income ≤ €40,000 (bonus mamme).
policies.caveat: Both are recent (2025) and budget-dependent; the birth bonus must be claimed within 60 days of birth, and the bonus mamme was €40/month in 2025 and paid in a lump sum in December.

LT.note: Lithuania combines a long, well-paid leave (maternity 77.58% uncapped, then 60% of pay until the child is 18 months, with 2 months reserved per parent) with a universal 'child money' payment of €129.50 per child and a €1,036 birth grant from June 2026. A municipal kindergarten place is guaranteed by law from age 2 since 2025 and costs only tens of euros a month in Vilnius. There are no child tax credits (replaced by child money in 2018) and no rent support at median wage; the generous 20–25% first-home subsidy for young families is only available outside the big cities and is rationed by budget. Lithuania takes a heavy 19.5% employee social contribution and only a wage-tapered tax-free amount from median pay (a €1,044 per-child tax-free amount returns in 2027), but its Labour Code is unusually parent-friendly: each parent of two under-12s gets 12 extra paid days a year and an enforceable right to part-time and remote work until the child turns 8.

headline.cash: €259/month for 2 kids (child money €129.50 each) + €1,036 birth grant from June 2026
headline.leave: maternity 126 days at 77.58% uncapped; 30 days paternity; 2 non-transferable months each at 77.58%, then 60% until child is 18 months (or 45%/30% to 24 months)
headline.childcare: municipal kindergarten place guaranteed from age 2 (since 2025); Vilnius fee €26/month + meals ≈ €3–4/day; pre-primary and grades 1–2 meals free
headline.tax: none — child tax allowances were replaced by universal child money in 2018
headline.labourtax: 20% PIT with a wage-tapered tax-free amount (NPD €747 max, ≈ €380/month at median pay ≈ €900/yr saved); €1,044/yr extra NPD per child from 2027; employee Sodra 19.5%
headline.workrights: 20 working days leave + 16 holidays; parents of 2 under-12s get 1 paid day off per month each; right to part-time and remote work until child is 8

policies.name: Maternity, paternity and child-care benefit (Sodra)
policies.what: Maternity: 126 days (70 before, 56 after) at 77.58% of insured pay, no ceiling. Paternity: 30 days at 77.58%. Child-care benefit: each parent 2 non-transferable months at 77.58% (max €3,768/month Q1 2026), then 60% until the child is 18 months, or 45% for 12 months then 30% to 24 months. Ceiling 2x average wage (≈ €4,831), floor €560–592.
policies.value: ≈ €1,475/month during maternity and the reserved months, then ≈ €1,140/month at a €1,900 gross wage; roughly €22,000 gross per child over 18 months
policies.eligibility: 12 months of social insurance in the last 24 months; both parents must be insured to use both non-transferable blocks.
policies.caveat: Duration option is fixed once chosen. Earnings while on child-care leave reduce the benefit (except in the non-transferable months). Uninsured parents get a flat €444/month until age 2 from June 2026.

policies.name: Child money (išmoka vaikui) + one-off childbirth grant
policies.what: Universal, non-means-tested €129.50/month per child (1.75 x basic social benefit of €74, 2026) from birth to 18 (23 if in school). An extra €76.22/month per child only for families with 3+ children, a disabled child or income under €352/person. One-off grant per newborn: €814, rising to 14 basic social benefits = €1,036 for births from 1 June 2026.
policies.value: €259/month for 2 kids (€3,108/year) plus €1,036 per birth from June 2026
policies.eligibility: All children permanently resident in Lithuania; apply once via spis.lt or the municipality.
policies.url_label: Ministry of Social Security and Labour — benefits for children
policies.caveat: A two-earner median family does not qualify for the €76 supplement. Indexed only through the basic social benefit (€70 → €74 in 2026).

policies.name: Guaranteed municipal kindergarten place from age 2, low fees
policies.what: Since 2025 the Education Law obliges municipalities to provide an early-education place for every child from age 2 (phased in from age 4 in 2023). Vilnius municipal kindergartens charge a €26/month education fee (€13 for social-benefit recipients) plus meals of roughly €3–4 per attended day. One year of pre-primary is compulsory from the year the child turns 6 (5 allowed) with free meals.
policies.value: ≈ €90–110/month per child in Vilnius (fee + meals), two kids ≈ €200/month
policies.eligibility: Children registered in the municipality; admission via the municipal e-system (Vilnius: darželiai.vilnius.lt).
policies.url_label: Eurydice — early childhood education and care in Lithuania
policies.caveat: The guarantee is a place somewhere in the municipality, not in the preferred kindergarten; Vilnius and Kaunas suburbs still have queues for 1–2 year olds. Fees differ by municipality.

policies.name: Extra paid days off for parents of children under 12 (mamadienis / tėvadienis)
policies.what: Labour Code art. 138(3): an employee raising one child under 12 gets one additional paid rest day every three months (or 8 fewer hours per quarter); with two children under 12 (or one disabled child under 18) one paid day per month or a 2-hour shorter week; with three or more, two days per month. Paid at the employee's average wage and available to each parent separately.
policies.value: 2 kids: 12 paid days a year per parent, 24 per household ≈ €2,100 gross at a ~€1,900 wage; 1 kid: 4 days per parent
policies.eligibility: All employees under the Labour Code raising a child under 12; taken on request, can be accumulated for shift workers.
policies.caveat: Stops when the younger child turns 12 (drops to one day per quarter once only one child is under 12); employer pays, so some small firms resist. Sick-child days are separate: Sodra pays roughly 66% from day 1 for up to 14 days per illness for a child under 14 (2026).

policies.name: Tax-free amount (NPD) on wages + €1,044 per-child NPD from 2027
policies.what: PIT on employment income is 20% (25%/32% only above 36 and 60 average wages, 2026). A monthly tax-free amount of €747 applies up to the €1,153 minimum wage and tapers by €0.49 per euro above it: NPD = 747 − 0.49 × (wage − 1,153), zero at ≈ €2,677. From 1 January 2027 an additional NPD of €1,044 per year per child under 18 is reintroduced for wage-earning parents.
policies.value: ≈ €381/month tax-free at a ~€1,900 gross wage → ≈ €914/year less tax per earner (€1,828 for two); +€209/year per child from 2027 (€418 for 2 kids, claimable by one parent)
policies.eligibility: Resident employees; applied monthly by the employer on request and reconciled in the annual return. The child NPD needs the child registered as a dependant.
policies.url_label: VMI (State Tax Inspectorate) — NPD and additional NPD (art. 20)
policies.caveat: Employee Sodra contributions of 19.5% (12.52% pension + 6.98% health) come on top and are not reduced for parents; the NPD taper means each extra euro earned between €1,153 and €2,677 is effectively taxed at ≈ 30% plus contributions.

policies.name: Financial incentive for young families buying a first home
policies.what: State subsidy paid to the bank against a first-home mortgage for families where both spouses (or the single parent) are under 36: 15% of the loan with no children, 20% with one child, 25% with two, 30% with three or more, calculated on a loan of up to €87,000. Can be used as the down payment. Not available in the largest cities and their neighbouring municipalities.
policies.value: Up to €21,750 (25% of an €87,000 loan) for a 2-child family buying outside Vilnius/Kaunas/Klaipėda
policies.eligibility: Under 36, no home owned, first home in an eligible regional municipality, mortgage approved by a participating bank.
policies.url_label: Seimas — Law on the Financial Incentive for Young Families Acquiring a First Home (EN)
policies.caveat: Annual budget is capped (≈ €5.6m allocated in May 2026) and certificates go on a first-come basis, so applications open for a day and queue. Useless for a family that must stay in a big city for work.

policies.name: Right to part-time and remote work until the child is 8; 20 days leave + 16 public holidays
policies.what: Labour Code art. 40(5): the normal limits on requesting part-time (3 years' tenure, max 1 year) do not apply to an employee raising a child under 8, who may switch to part-time and back. Art. 52(2): the employer must grant a remote-work request from a parent of a child under 8 unless it proves excessive cost. Annual leave is at least 20 working days (25 for single parents of an under-14) plus 16 public holidays (art. 123).
policies.value: Enforceable reduced hours and home-working for both parents for 8 years per child; ≈ 4 weeks leave + up to 16 paid holidays per year
policies.eligibility: All employees under the Labour Code; written request, no firm-size threshold.
policies.caveat: Part-time is paid pro rata; the remote-work duty applies only to jobs that can be done remotely and employers can invoke 'production necessity'. Several public holidays (Easter Sunday, Mother's and Father's Day) always fall on Sundays.

policies.name: Free school and pre-primary meals, free child health cover
policies.what: All pre-primary pupils and pupils in grades 1–2 get free school meals regardless of income; older pupils only if family income is under €349.50/person. Children under 18 are covered by compulsory health insurance at state expense, with free GP, hospital and dental care in the public system, and textbooks are free.
policies.value: ≈ €40–60/month saved per child in pre-primary/grades 1–2 on meals; €0 for public health care
policies.eligibility: All children resident in Lithuania.
policies.url_label: Ministry of Social Security and Labour — free school meals
policies.caveat: Universal free meals stop after grade 2; the €148 school-supplies grant is means-tested and out of reach at median income.

LU.note: For a two-earner family with small children Luxembourg is probably the most generous country in Europe: each parent can take up to 6 months of parental leave paid at close to full salary (max €4,619/month), crèche is free for 20 hours a week from age 1, child benefit is over €300 per child and school-age care, meals, books and all public transport are free. The weak point is housing: rents are among the highest in the EU and the rent subsidy is out of reach for a median two-earner household. Amounts are index-linked and rose in June 2026. Luxembourg also takes comparatively little out of wages (employee contributions of about 12.5%, a tax credit for every employee and completely tax-free overtime) and pairs it with strong workplace rights: 26 days' leave, eleven holidays, 12–18 paid days per child per year for a sick child and near-universal meal vouchers. Luxembourg also takes comparatively little out of wages (employee contributions of about 12.5%, a tax credit for every employee and completely tax-free overtime) and pairs it with strong workplace rights: 26 days' leave, eleven holidays, a paid budget of 12–18 days per child to nurse a sick child and near-universal meal vouchers.

headline.cash: €630/month for 2 kids (allocation familiale €315.04 each, June 2026) + €1,740 birth grant
headline.leave: 20 weeks maternity at 100%; parental leave 4–6 months per parent at €2,771–€4,619/month; 10 days paternity
headline.childcare: 20 h/week free crèche ages 1–4 (46 weeks/year); income-capped fees beyond; free school-age care and lunch from 4
headline.tax: joint taxation (class 2) for married couples; child bonus folded into the family allowance
headline.labourtax: employee contributions ≈ 12.5%; €600 employee tax credit (tapering to 0 at €80,000); overtime pay fully income-tax-free; brackets raised 2.5 index tranches in 2024 and 2025
headline.workrights: 26 days paid leave + 11 holidays; paid sick-child leave 12 days per child under 4, 18 days age 4–13; tax-free meal vouchers €15/day

policies.name: Congé parental (paid parental leave, each parent)
policies.what: Each parent has an individual, non-transferable right per child: 4 or 6 months full-time, 8 or 12 months half-time, or split over up to 20 months. The CAE pays average earnings of the previous 12 months, between €2,771.33 and €4,618.88/month full-time (index June 2026). One parent starts right after maternity leave; the other before the child turns 6.
policies.value: ≈ €4,000–4,600/month for 6 months per parent at median pay, i.e. up to ≈ €50,000+ per child if both parents take full leave
policies.eligibility: Employed or self-employed, insured in Luxembourg for 12 continuous months before the leave, working at least 10 h/week.
policies.caveat: Part-time formulas need employer agreement; the second parent's leave is lost if not taken before age 6.

policies.name: Chèque-service accueil (CSA): 20 free hours + income-capped crèche fees
policies.what: Children aged 1–4 in an accredited crèche, mini-crèche or (from 2026) childminder get 20 hours/week free for 46 weeks/year regardless of income. Beyond that the State pays up to €7/hour (since Jan 2026), parents an income-graded share; meals capped near €4.50. The 2026 reform makes care fully free below 2× minimum wage and promises every child a place by 2030.
policies.value: ≈ €6,400/year per child in free hours (≈ €12,900 for 2 kids); a full-time crèche place then costs a median family roughly €300–600/month net
policies.eligibility: Resident children from 1 year until school entry (children of cross-border workers also eligible); parents must register for the CSA with their commune.
policies.caveat: Places are unevenly distributed regionally; parents who do not disclose income pay the maximum tariff; under-1s are not covered by the free hours.

policies.name: Allocation pour l'avenir des enfants (family allowance) + birth grant
policies.what: Universal monthly child benefit of €315.04 per child (index 992.24, from 1 June 2026), rising by €23.81 from age 6 and €59.44 from age 12, plus a back-to-school allowance from age 6. Birth grant of 3 × €580.03 (prenatal, birth, postnatal) tied to medical check-ups. Indexed to prices since 2021.
policies.value: €630/month (≈ €7,560/year) for 2 kids under 6, plus ≈ €1,740 per birth
policies.eligibility: Every child legally resident in Luxembourg (and children of cross-border workers); paid by the CAE, no income test.
policies.caveat: Single flat amount per child since 2016 (no higher rate for larger families); the former child tax bonus is already included in it.

policies.name: Congé de maternité + congé de paternité
policies.what: Maternity leave of 20 weeks (8 before, 12 after birth) paid by the CNS at 100% of the highest salary of the previous 3 months, capped at 5× the social minimum wage (≈ €13,800/month). Fathers or second parents get 10 paid days of paternity leave, the first 2 paid by the employer and the rest reimbursed by the State.
policies.value: ≈ 4.6 months of full salary per birth for the mother, 2 weeks for the father
policies.eligibility: Insured employees and self-employed with 6 months of affiliation in the year before the leave; dismissal protected.
policies.caveat: Followed directly by the first parent's parental leave if that option is chosen; no extension for breastfeeding beyond daily breaks.

policies.name: Free school-age care and lunches, free public transport, free schoolbooks
policies.what: Since September 2022 the maison relais (after-school care) and lunch are free during school weeks for all children in compulsory education (from age 4, précoce from 3), regardless of income. All public transport has been free nationwide since March 2020, including for children. Compulsory schoolbooks are free in secondary school.
policies.value: Roughly €300–500/month saved per school-age child on care and meals, plus zero transport costs for the whole family
policies.eligibility: All children attending school in Luxembourg; care requires CSA registration with the commune.
policies.url_label: MEN — Gratuité de l'accueil et des repas
policies.caveat: Free care applies to school weeks only; holiday care still carries an income-graded CSA fee.

policies.name: Congé pour raisons familiales (paid sick-child leave) + 100% employer sick pay
policies.what: Each working parent may take paid leave to care for a sick child: 12 days per child over ages 0–4, 18 days per child over ages 4–13 and 5 days (hospitalisation) over 13–18; the employer pays full salary and is reimbursed by the Mutualité des employeurs, capped at 5× the social minimum wage. For the parent's own illness the employer continues 100% pay until the end of the month in which the 77th sick day (in 18 months) falls, then the CNS pays.
policies.value: 24 paid days per parent while 2 children are under 4 (12 per child), then 36 days per parent for ages 4–13; full pay for up to ~3 months of own illness
policies.eligibility: Employees and self-employed insured in Luxembourg; medical certificate required; both parents cannot take the leave on the same day.
policies.url_label: guichet.lu — Leave for family reasons (sick child)
policies.caveat: The days are a budget per child for the whole age band, not per year (12 days for the entire 0–4 period, extendable only with a medical certificate of exceptional need); parents who often nurse sick toddlers exhaust it quickly.

policies.name: 26 days' leave, 11 public holidays, tax-free meal vouchers and flexible-work requests
policies.what: Statutory paid leave is 26 working days for everyone (public sector 32), plus 11 paid public holidays with a compensatory day when one falls on a weekend. Meal vouchers (chèques-repas) of up to €15 per working day are exempt from tax and contributions except for the employee's €2.80 share (since 2024). Since 2023 parents of children under 9 may request flexible or remote working arrangements and the employer must answer in writing; a right to disconnect must be laid down in every company.
policies.value: 37 paid days off per year per parent; meal vouchers worth ≈ €2,600 net per earner per year (≈ 18 × €12.20 × 12) where offered
policies.eligibility: All employees under the Labour Code; meal vouchers depend on the employer (very common in Luxembourg); flexible-work request needs 6 months' tenure.
policies.caveat: The flexible-work request can be refused with reasons; meal vouchers are a widespread but voluntary employer benefit.

policies.name: Crédit d'impôt pour salariés (CIS) + tax-free overtime + low employee contributions
policies.what: Every employee gets a tax credit paid through payroll: €600/year for gross pay of €11,265–40,000, tapering by €0.015 per euro above €40,000 to zero at €80,000 (2026). Overtime pay — the base hour and the 40% supplement — is fully exempt from income tax (Art. 115 no. 11 LIR) and the supplement also from social contributions. Employee social contributions are only about 12.5% of gross (pension 8%, health 3.05%, dependency 1.4%).
policies.value: ≈ €250–400 CIS per earner per year at a median wage of roughly €55,000–62,000 (≈ €500–800 per household); every hour of overtime is paid 140% net of income tax
policies.eligibility: All employees with a Luxembourg tax card (CIS automatic); overtime exemption applies to legally recognised overtime of non-executive staff.
policies.caveat: The CIS phases out exactly across the median-wage range, so a two-earner household above €80,000 each gets nothing; overtime is capped at 2 hours/day and 10 hours/week and executives are excluded.

policies.name: Bracket indexation (2024–2025) and the tax-favoured prime pour jeunes salariés
policies.what: The tax scale was raised by 2.5 index tranches on 1 January 2024 and again by 2.5 tranches on 1 January 2025 (Entlaaschtungs-Pak), lifting the zero-rate threshold to €13,230 and pushing all brackets up by about 10% in two years. Since 2025 an employer may pay employees under 30 on their first permanent contract a 'young-employee bonus' of which 75% is tax-free, up to €5,000/year for pay below €50,000 (€3,750 up to €75,000), for 5 years.
policies.value: Indexation is worth roughly €500–800 per earner per year at a median wage compared with the 2023 scale; the youth bonus is worth up to ≈ €1,500 in tax saved per year if the employer pays it and the parent is still under 30
policies.eligibility: Indexation: all taxpayers. Youth bonus: under 30 on 1 January, first permanent contract signed from 2025, employer must choose to pay it.
policies.url_label: Administration des contributions directes — Prime jeune salarié
policies.caveat: Luxembourg has no automatic indexation of the tax scale — wages are indexed automatically, brackets are not, so fiscal drag returns whenever the government pauses; no adjustment was made for 2026. The youth bonus is employer-discretionary and ends at 30.

official.label: Caisse pour l'avenir des enfants (CAE) — family benefits and parental leave

guide.label: EU Your Europe — Family benefits

LV.note: Latvia pays earnings-related leave at lower rates than its neighbours (80% maternity, then 60% or 43.75% parental benefit), but layers a flat child-care allowance on top, which jumped from €171 to €298/month in 2026, and a €600 birth grant. Municipal kindergarten is legally guaranteed from 18 months and tuition-free (parents pay meals); Riga currently reports no waiting list, though it is cutting co-funding of private places. The €250/month tax allowance per dependant is worth about €64 per child; a state mortgage guarantee for families with children is the only housing lever and requires a loan, not savings. Latvia's 2025 tax reform replaced the phased-out allowance with a flat €550/month tax-free amount for every earner but raised the bottom rate to 25.5%, so a median earner gains only a few hundred euros a year, while the Labour Law gives parents of under-14s an enforceable right to part-time work and the state pays 80% sickness benefit from the first day a child is ill.

headline.cash: €298/month child-care allowance until 18 months + family state benefit (€25 for 1 child, €100 for 2) + €600 birth grant (2026)
headline.leave: maternity 112 days at 80%; parental benefit 60% until child is 1 (or 43.75% until 1.5), incl. 2 non-transferable months per parent; 10 days paternity at 80%
headline.childcare: municipal kindergarten place guaranteed from 18 months, tuition-free; meals ≈ €2.15/day in Riga after city co-funding
headline.tax: €250/month per child off taxable income (≈ €64/child/month at the 25.5% rate)
headline.labourtax: fixed €550/month non-taxable minimum since 2025 (≈ €1,680/yr per earner at the 25.5% rate); employee social contributions 10.5%; no earned-income credit
headline.workrights: 4 weeks leave + 1 extra day for parents + 15 public holidays; legal right to part-time until child is 14; sick-child benefit 80% from day 1

policies.name: Maternity, paternity and parental benefit (vecāku pabalsts)
policies.what: Maternity benefit: 112 days (56+56, up to 140) at 80% of insured earnings, no cap. Paternity: 10 working days at 80%. Parental benefit: 60% of average insured earnings until the child is 1 (13 months incl. 2 non-transferable months per parent) or 43.75% until 1.5 (19 months). Father's 2 months usable until age 8.
policies.value: ≈ €900/month at a €1,500 gross wage for 13 months (60% option) ≈ €11,700 per child, plus 80% during 112 maternity days
policies.eligibility: Employees/self-employed with contributions in 3 of the last 6 months or 6 of the last 24.
policies.caveat: Option cannot be changed once chosen. Working while on parental benefit reduces it to 75% in 2026. For births from 2026 only maternity-leave days count towards the parental benefit period.

policies.name: Child-care allowance (bērna kopšanas pabalsts) + family state benefit + birth grant
policies.what: Flat child-care allowance of €298/month for every child under 18 months (raised from €171 in 2026), then €42.69 to age 2, paid on top of parental benefit to the same parent. Family state benefit from age 1: €25/month for one child, €100 for two, €225 for three. One-off childbirth allowance €600 for births from 1 Jan 2026 (was €421.17).
policies.value: ≈ €325–400/month in the newborn's first year (€298 + €25–100) plus €600 at birth; €100/month once both kids are over 1
policies.eligibility: Permanent residents registered with the child; no income test.
policies.caveat: Payment for the 1.5–2 year band is being phased out for children born after 2 Nov 2026. Family state benefit only starts at the child's first birthday and is tiny for one child.

policies.name: Fixed non-taxable minimum of €550/month for all earners (2026)
policies.what: Since 1 January 2025 every employee gets a flat tax-free amount instead of the old income-differentiated minimum that fell to zero at €1,800/month: €510/month in 2025, €550/month (€6,600/year) in 2026. PIT on employment income is 25.5% up to €105,300/year and 33% above; employee social contributions are 10.5% of gross pay.
policies.value: ≈ €1,683/year less income tax per earner (€3,366 for two earners) at 25.5%; net gain vs the 2024 rules at a €1,500 gross wage roughly €500/year per earner because the bottom rate rose from 20% to 25.5%
policies.eligibility: All resident employees; the employer applies it automatically to whoever holds the electronic wage-tax booklet (one employer only).
policies.url_label: Ministry of Finance — non-taxable minimum and tax allowances
policies.caveat: Not indexed beyond the announced €550 for 2026; the flat 25.5% rate means Latvia taxes median wages harder than Estonia (22% with a €700 exemption and 3.6% employee contributions).

policies.name: Personal income tax allowance for dependants
policies.what: Each dependent child reduces the claiming parent's taxable income by €250/month (€3,000/year) on top of the fixed €550/month non-taxable minimum; PIT rate is 25.5% up to €105,300/year (2025–2026). Applied monthly by the employer via the electronic wage tax book.
policies.value: ≈ €127.50/month more net pay for 2 kids (≈ €1,530/year)
policies.eligibility: Any working parent registering the child as a dependant in the VID EDS system; only one parent per child.
policies.url_label: Ministry of Finance — non-taxable minimum and tax allowances
policies.caveat: Allowance frozen at €250 since 2021 despite inflation; worth nothing if the parent's income is already below the non-taxable minimum.

policies.name: Tuition-free municipal kindergarten from 18 months
policies.what: Education Law entitles every child from 1.5 years to a place in a municipal pre-school; tuition is free, parents pay only meals. In Riga three meals cost €4.30/day with the city paying half (€2.15) for Riga-registered children. If the municipality cannot offer a place it must co-finance a private kindergarten (Riga ~€300+/month).
policies.value: ≈ €45/month per child for meals in Riga; two kids in municipal kindergarten ≈ €90/month
policies.eligibility: Children registered in the municipality; co-financing only for Riga-declared children.
policies.url_label: Riga City — kindergarten and school meal support
policies.caveat: Riga says it has no waiting list in 2026 but plans to halve private-kindergarten co-funding where municipal places exist; smaller municipalities and Pierīga can still have shortages for 1.5–3 year olds.

policies.name: Sickness benefit for caring for a sick child (80% from day 1)
policies.what: When a child under 14 is ill, the doctor issues the parent a sick-leave certificate B from the first day and the State Social Insurance Agency (VSAA) pays 80% of the parent's average insured earnings for up to 14 days per illness at home (21 days if partly in hospital, 30 days for bone fractures). Grandparents or adult siblings can take it if the parents cannot.
policies.value: ≈ €39/day (80% of a €1,500 gross wage) for every sick-child day, up to 14 days per illness, no cap on the number of illnesses per year
policies.eligibility: Employed or self-employed parent (or guardian) who loses income while caring; claim within 6 months via Latvija.gov.lv.
policies.url_label: VSAA — sickness benefit if a child is ill
policies.caveat: Paid on last year's average insured earnings, taxed, and only if the parent earns nothing that day; the parent's own sick pay is lower (employer pays 75% on days 2–3, 80% on days 4–9).

policies.name: Right to part-time work until the child is 14 + 4 weeks leave and an extra day for parents
policies.what: Labour Law s.134(2): the employer must set part-time hours when requested by an employee with a child under 14 (or under 18 if disabled), with a right to return to full time; refusal to switch cannot justify dismissal. Annual paid leave is at least 4 calendar weeks (s.149) plus one supplementary paid day for employees with one or two children under 14 (s.151), plus 15 public holidays (several fall on Sundays in a given year).
policies.value: Enforceable reduced hours for both parents for 14 years; ≈ 21 paid leave days + 13–15 holidays per parent per year
policies.eligibility: All employees under the Labour Law; part-time request in writing, no minimum firm size or tenure.
policies.url_label: Likumi.lv — Labour Law (official English translation), ss. 134, 149, 151
policies.caveat: Part-time means proportionally lower pay; there is no equivalent statutory right to remote work (s.76 only regulates cost reimbursement once remote work is agreed) and no state-paid child-leave days as in Estonia.

policies.name: ALTUM state mortgage guarantee for families with children
policies.what: State guarantee replacing part of the down payment on a first-home loan: in Riga, Pierīga and Jūrmala 10% of the loan (max €10,000) with one child, 15% (max €15,000) with two; outside those areas 30–40%. Lets banks finance up to 95% of the property value on transactions up to €300,000; guarantee runs 10 years.
policies.value: Buy a €150,000 flat with ≈ €7,500 own savings instead of €22,500+ (2 kids, Riga)
policies.eligibility: Families with children up to 23 or expecting a baby, regular income but insufficient savings; needs a bank mortgage approval.
policies.url_label: ALTUM — housing guarantees for families with children
policies.caveat: It is a guarantee, not a grant: the family still repays the full loan and pays a guarantee fee. The 'Balsts' cash subsidy is only for families with 3+ children or a disabled child. No rent allowance exists at median income.

official.label: VSAA — State Social Insurance Agency (family benefits)

guide.label: European Commission — Your social security rights in Latvia

MT.note: Malta's stand-out policy for a dual-earner couple is the Free Childcare Scheme: full-time childcare from 3 months to 3 years at no cost for working parents, followed by free state kindergarten from 3. Cash support is modest at a median wage (about €1,090 per child per year plus a birth bonus) and paid parental leave beyond maternity is short and low-paid. Because most young Maltese buy rather than rent, the state leans on first-time-buyer help (10% deposit scheme, €1,000/yr grant, stamp-duty exemption) rather than rent subsidies, which are only for low incomes. Malta keeps deductions from a median pay-cheque low (10% social security plus parent tax rates) and tops it up with a symbolic yearly refund cheque and flat 10–15% rates on part-time and overtime pay, but conciliation rights stop at a right to request flexible work and a modest 24 days of leave.

headline.cash: ≈ €2,180/yr for 2 kids above the €30,000 income threshold (Children's Allowance ≈ €450 + €640 supplement per child, 2026); €1,000/€1,500 birth bonus
headline.leave: 18 weeks maternity (14 at full pay, 4 at €213.54/wk) + 10 days paternity at full pay; parental leave 4 months each, only 2 paid at ~50% of sickness benefit
headline.childcare: Free Childcare Scheme 3 months–3 years for working parents (up to ~210 h/month); free state kindergarten from 3
headline.tax: parent rates 2026: first €18,500 tax-free with 2+ children (vs €12,000 single), 15% to €25,500, 25% to €60,000
headline.labourtax: employee SS 10% capped at €55.93/week (2026); yearly 'tax refund' cheque €60–140 per worker; 10% flat tax on part-time, 15% on overtime (first €10,000)
headline.workrights: 24 days leave + 14 holidays (weekend holidays added since 2021); right to REQUEST flexible work until child is 8; 32 h urgent family leave

policies.name: Free Childcare Scheme (3 months–3 years)
policies.what: Government pays fees at registered childcare centres for children aged 3 months to 3 years when both parents work (or study). Entitlement is 110% of one parent's monthly working hours plus 20 hours/month for commuting, i.e. about 210 hours/month for full-timers. Run by Jobsplus (new 4-year €276m contract, 2025). From age 3, state kindergarten is free.
policies.value: ≈ €400–600/month per child saved versus private fees (≈ €10,000–14,000/yr for two children)
policies.eligibility: Both parents (or a single parent) in employment paying social security, or in recognised education; child registered at a participating centre.
policies.caveat: Places at popular centres fill up early (register during pregnancy); hours beyond the entitlement, meals and extras are billed; eligibility ends the term the child turns 3.

policies.name: Parent income-tax rates (new 2026 bands)
policies.what: A parent who maintains a child under 18 (23 if in full-time education) is taxed at parent rates. Budget 2026 split these by family size: with 2+ children the first €18,500 is tax-free, 15% to €25,500, 25% to €60,000, 35% above (one child: €14,500 / €21,000). Single rates start taxing at €12,000. Married-rates version: €22,500 tax-free with 2+ children.
policies.value: roughly €1,000–1,500/yr less tax at a median wage compared with single rates (2026), on top of general 2025 band cuts
policies.eligibility: Resident parents with dependent children; chosen on the annual return (or via FSS on the payslip).
policies.url_label: Malta Tax & Customs Administration — New tax rates 2026 (PDF)
policies.caveat: Only one computation applies per return: a married couple either uses joint married rates or one spouse uses parent rates and the other single rates; the government has said the new bands are set for three years.

policies.name: Maternity leave, paternity leave and parental leave
policies.what: Maternity: 18 weeks, first 14 at full pay from the employer, last 4 paid by government at €213.54/week (2026); 6 weeks after birth compulsory. Paternity: 10 working days at full pay. Parental leave: 4 months per parent per child until age 8; 2 months non-transferable, paid at 50% of the sickness-benefit rate for under-4s (about €80–95/week), the rest unpaid.
policies.value: ≈ 3.5 months of full pay for the mother + 2 weeks for the father per birth; paid parental leave adds only ≈ €700–800 per parent
policies.eligibility: All employees (parental leave after 12 months' service); self-employed mothers get a flat maternity benefit instead.
policies.url_label: DIER — Maternity leave (Department of Industrial and Employment Relations)
policies.caveat: Beyond 14 weeks the mother's income drops to roughly the minimum wage, and shared parental leave is close to unpaid, so most families rely on the free childcare scheme from month 4–5.

policies.name: Vacation leave, public holidays, urgent family leave and carers' leave
policies.what: Full-timers get at least 192 hours (24 days) paid annual leave plus 14 paid public holidays; since 2021 holidays falling on weekends are added as extra leave days. Plus 32 hours a year of paid urgent family leave (deducted from leave/sick leave), 5 days unpaid carers' leave, 2+ weeks paid sick leave.
policies.value: ≈ 26–28 paid days off + 14 holidays per earner in 2026, all at full pay
policies.eligibility: All whole-time employees (pro rata for part-time); carers' leave and urgent family leave from day one.
policies.url_label: DIER — Vacation leave (Department of Industrial and Employment Relations)
policies.caveat: Employers may use up to 12 days of the entitlement for shutdowns; sick leave beyond the sectoral minimum (often 2–4 weeks) drops to the flat social-security sickness benefit.

policies.name: Annual 'tax refund' cheque and low, capped employee social security contributions
policies.what: Budget 2026 again sent every employee earning under €60,000 a cheque of €60 to €140 (largest for the lowest incomes; ≈ 280,000 recipients, November 2025). Employee social security is a flat 10% of basic wage, capped at €55.93/week (2026) above €29,084, with no separate health or unemployment premium; the 2025/26 budgets widened the tax-free band to €12,000 (single).
policies.value: ≈ €150–250/yr in refund cheques for two median earners; ≈ €2,200/yr of contributions each on a €22,000 wage (10%)
policies.eligibility: Cheque: employed in the reference year with income under €60,000, automatic by post; contributions: all Class 1 employees.
policies.url_label: Ministry for Finance — Budget 2026 (speech and documents)
policies.caveat: The cheque is a discretionary yearly hand-out, not a tax rule, and its value has been flat since 2022; the 10% contribution has no ceiling relief for median wages.

policies.name: Right to request flexible working arrangements for parents (Work-Life Balance Regulations, L.N. 201/2022)
policies.what: Since 2 Aug 2022 employees with a child up to 8, and carers, may request flexible working arrangements for caring purposes (remote work, adjusted or reduced hours); the employer must consider the request, give reasons for any refusal or postponement, and allow a return to the original pattern afterwards. The same regulations brought 10 days' paid paternity leave.
policies.value: no cash value; in practice mainly public-sector and larger private employers grant reduced hours or telework, letting both parents keep jobs while the free childcare hours run out
policies.eligibility: Employees with a child under 8 or caring responsibilities; a qualifying period of up to 6 months' service may be required.
policies.caveat: It is only a right to ask and get a written answer, not a right to part-time as in Spain or Portugal; refusals on business grounds are lawful.

policies.name: 10% flat tax on part-time income and 15% on overtime (first €10,000 each)
policies.what: Income from a qualifying part-time job (alongside a main job, or as a parent/pensioner) is taxed at a flat 10% on the first €10,000 a year (max €1,000 tax) instead of progressive rates; qualifying overtime at 15% on the first €10,000 (max €1,500) for non-managerial employees with a basic wage ≤ €375/week (≈ €19,500/yr). Both since 1 Jan 2022.
policies.value: ≈ €1,000–1,500/yr saved per earner who does part-time or overtime on top of a median job; nothing for a plain full-time salary
policies.eligibility: Part-time: separate qualifying employment registered with Jobsplus; overtime: basic wage ≤ €375/week, non-managerial; both elective.
policies.url_label: Malta Tax & Customs Administration — FSS update: part-time and overtime tax from 2022
policies.caveat: A median full-time basic wage (≈ €21,000–22,000) already sits above the €375/week overtime threshold, so for this household the 15% rate mostly does not apply; the 10% rate needs a second, separate job.

policies.name: Children's Allowance + Children's Allowance Supplement + Child Birth Bonus
policies.what: Means-tested Children's Allowance: at household income above €30,000 (2026 threshold, up from €27,434) a flat minimum of €8.66/week ≈ €450/yr per child; up to €27.29/week (≈ €1,419/yr) at very low incomes. Since 2025 a supplement adds €640/yr per child above the threshold (€910 below), paid quarterly. One-off birth bonus (2026): €1,000 first child, €1,500 second, €2,000 third+.
policies.value: ≈ €2,180/yr (≈ €180/month) for two children at two median wages, plus €2,500 in birth bonuses for a first and second child
policies.eligibility: Parents resident in Malta with children under 16 (21 if in education/registering unemployed); automatic yearly means test.
policies.url_label: Social Security Malta — Children's Allowance (income exceeds threshold)
policies.caveat: Two full-time earners almost always exceed the €30,000 threshold, so they get the flat minimum; the In-Work Benefit for couples stops at about €36,850 combined income.

policies.name: 10% Deposit Scheme + First-Time Buyer grant and stamp-duty exemption
policies.what: Housing Authority arranges a bank loan for the 10% deposit on a first home worth up to €250,000 (Budget 2026) for buyers aged 21–39 who qualify for a mortgage but lack savings; the Authority pays the interest, so only capital is repaid over 25 years. First-time buyers also get €1,000/yr for 10 years and pay no stamp duty below €200,000.
policies.value: ≈ €25,000 deposit financed interest-free + €10,000 grant + up to €7,000 duty saved; rent subsidies exist only for low incomes
policies.eligibility: First-time buyers resident in Malta, 21–39 for the deposit scheme, property ≤ €250,000, bank loan approval.
policies.caveat: €250,000 buys little near Valletta/Sliema, so the scheme mainly helps in cheaper localities or Gozo; a two-median-income couple still needs a mortgage of ~€225,000, roughly 5× joint income.

official.label: Social Security Malta — Families and children (benefits timeline)

guide.label: European Commission — Your social security rights in Malta

NL.note: For a two-earner family the Netherlands works through one big lever: the kinderopvangtoeslag, which refunds 79-92% of daycare costs even at a household income of about €90,000, provided both parents work. Everything else is modest: child benefit of about €200/month for two kids, an income-tested kindgebonden budget that is mostly phased out at two median wages, and leave beyond the mother's 16 weeks paid at only 70%. Housing benefit is out of reach at this income, daycare places have waiting lists, and many providers charge above the subsidised hourly rate, so the parents' own share is often higher than the tables suggest. Labour is taxed lightly at a median wage thanks to the arbeidskorting worth over €11,000 a year for the couple, and Dutch law makes part-time and adjusted hours an enforceable right rather than a favour, which is why most Dutch parents of small children work 3-4 days.

headline.cash: ≈ €199/month for 2 kids under 6 (kinderbijslag €298.40/quarter each, from July 2026) + kindgebonden budget ≈ €0-2,500/yr depending on hours
headline.leave: 16 weeks maternity at 100%; partner 1 week 100% + 5 weeks 70%; 9 weeks per parent at 70% in year 1
headline.childcare: kinderopvangtoeslag covers 78.9% (1st child) and 92.2% (2nd) of €11.23/hour at ≈ €90k household income (2026)
headline.tax: IACK up to €3,032/yr for the lower earner, but only if a child was born before 2025
headline.labourtax: arbeidskorting up to €5,685/earner (2026), still ≈ €5,500 at a median wage; brackets only partly indexed in 2026
headline.workrights: 20 days leave + 8% vakantiegeld; legal right to adjust hours/times (Wet flexibel werken, firms ≥10); 2 weeks sick-child leave at 70%; €0.25/km tax-free commuting

policies.name: Kinderopvangtoeslag (childcare benefit)
policies.what: Monthly refund of daycare costs for working parents, paid by Dienst Toeslagen. In 2026 it covers up to €11.23/hour (daycare) for max 230 hours/child/month; 96% at household income up to €56,413, still 78.9% for the 1st and 92.2% for the 2nd child at about €90,000, and never below 36.5%/68.2%. Parents pay only the remainder.
policies.value: ≈ €2,700/month subsidy for 2 kids in daycare 3 days/week at two median wages; parents pay ≈ €450-600/month
policies.eligibility: Both parents (or single parent) working or studying; hours capped at 140% of the lower earner's working hours; child in a registered provider.
policies.caveat: Many providers charge €12-13/hour, above the €11.23 subsidised rate, and urban waiting lists run 6-12 months. It is an advance based on estimated income, so over-payments are clawed back. A near-free (96% for all incomes) system has been announced but postponed; the government's stated target is 2029.

policies.name: Arbeidskorting (earned-income tax credit)
policies.what: A tax credit on income from work, built up to a maximum of €5,685 at €45,592 of earnings (2026) and then reduced by 6.51% of income above that, reaching zero at €132,921; applied automatically through payroll. Together with the algemene heffingskorting (€3,115 in 2026) it makes the first ≈ €25,000 of a median wage effectively tax-free.
policies.value: ≈ €5,500-5,685/year per earner at a median full-time wage (≈ €46,000) ≈ €11,000/year for the couple; a part-time second earner on €30,000 still gets ≈ €5,380
policies.eligibility: Everyone with income from employment or self-employment; no application needed.
policies.caveat: The 6.51% phase-out above €45,592 raises the marginal rate on extra hours to about 44%; 2026 bracket limits were indexed only partly (about half of inflation), and the IACK for the lower earner is being abolished for children born from 2025.

policies.name: Zwangerschapsverlof, geboorteverlof and betaald ouderschapsverlof
policies.what: Mother: 16 weeks maternity leave at 100% of pay (UWV, capped at the maximum daily wage, above a median salary). Partner: 1 week at full pay from the employer plus 5 weeks at 70% (UWV) within 6 months. Both parents: 9 weeks paid parental leave at 70% of daily wage (capped) in the first year, plus 17 unpaid weeks each.
policies.value: ≈ 16 weeks full pay + 6 weeks partner + 2 x 9 weeks at 70% per child for a median-wage couple
policies.eligibility: Employees; self-employed mothers get a separate ZEZ benefit. Employer applies to UWV.
policies.caveat: Paid parental leave must be used in the first year and is only 70%; the remaining 17 weeks per parent are unpaid unless a collective agreement tops up.

policies.name: Kinderbijslag (child benefit) + kindgebonden budget
policies.what: Kinderbijslag: universal, paid quarterly by SVB, €298.40 per child aged 0-5 from July 2026 (€362.35 at 6-11), no income test. Kindgebonden budget: income-tested top-up of up to about €2,580 per child under 12 (2026), reduced by 7.6% of household income above €39,141 for couples, so largely gone at two full-time median wages but ≈ €2,400/yr if one parent works part-time.
policies.value: ≈ €199/month for 2 small kids from kinderbijslag; kindgebonden budget ≈ €0-2,500/yr depending on hours worked
policies.eligibility: All residents with children (kinderbijslag); kindgebonden budget also has an asset limit for couples.
policies.caveat: Kinderbijslag is paid in arrears per quarter and is small by EU standards; the kindgebonden budget's phase-out rate was raised to 7.6% in 2026.

policies.name: Wet flexibel werken (right to adjust hours, times and workplace) + kortdurend zorgverlof at 70%
policies.what: After 26 weeks' service an employee can request fewer or more hours, different working times or a different workplace; the employer must grant a change of hours or times unless 'zwaarwegende bedrijfs- of dienstbelangen' oppose it (workplace requests only need serious consideration); firms under 10 staff must have their own scheme. Short-term care leave: up to 2x weekly hours per 12 months at ≥ 70% pay for a sick child; long-term care leave 6x weekly hours, unpaid.
policies.value: an enforceable 4-day or 3-day week (pay pro rata) for either parent + ≈ 2 weeks/year of sick-child leave at 70% pay per earner
policies.eligibility: Employees with 26 weeks' service; request in writing 2 months ahead; job and conditions otherwise unchanged.
policies.caveat: Reduced hours mean reduced pay and pension; the employer can refuse a workplace/home-working request on any reasonable ground; care leave may be topped up only by CAO.

policies.name: Statutory leave, 8% vakantiegeld, 2-year sick pay and tax-free commuting/home-working allowances
policies.what: Minimum paid leave is 4x weekly hours (20 days full-time) plus a statutory holiday allowance of at least 8% of gross annual wage paid in May/June; public holidays are not automatically free but nearly all CAOs grant them. Employers must pay at least 70% of wages for up to 2 years of sickness (most CAOs 100% in year 1). Tax-free reimbursements: commuting €0.25/km (2026, up from €0.23), home-working ≈ €2.40/day (2025), and free public-transport passes.
policies.value: ≈ €3,700/year vakantiegeld per earner at a median wage + 20 days leave + ≈ €1,000-2,000/year of untaxed commuting allowance at 20-40 km each way if the employer pays it
policies.eligibility: All employees (vakantiegeld and leave are statutory minima); allowances are at the employer's or CAO's discretion but almost universal.
policies.url_label: Rijksoverheid — Hoe hoog is mijn vakantiegeld?
policies.caveat: Vakantiegeld is part of the wage rather than a state benefit; 20 days is at the low end of the EU; sick-child and calamity leave beyond the 70% short-term care leave are unpaid.

policies.name: Inkomensafhankelijke combinatiekorting (IACK)
policies.what: Tax credit for the lower-earning working parent of a child under 12: 11.45% of earnings above €6,239, up to €3,032 (2026). It has been abolished for children born on or after 1 January 2025; families whose youngest qualifying child was born before 2025 keep it, with the maximum cut in 9 annual steps from 2027.
policies.value: up to ≈ €3,000/year for the lower earner, but only if the toddler was born before 2025; nothing for the newborn
policies.eligibility: Working parent earning above €6,239 with a co-resident child under 12 born before 2025, earning less than the partner.
policies.caveat: Being phased out: new parents get nothing, and existing recipients lose it stepwise 2027-2035. There is no family splitting or child tax credit otherwise.

official.label: Dienst Toeslagen — Kinderopvangtoeslag

guide.label: MISSOC — comparative tables on family benefits (EU)

NO.note: For a working couple Norway is among the most generous in Europe: 49 weeks of leave at 100% pay (up to 6G ≈ 819,000 kr, i.e. full replacement at median wage), a legal right to a barnehage place from age 1 at a capped 1,200 kr/month, and 20 paid sick-child days a year. The child benefit is modest and was flattened to one rate in Feb 2026; the housing allowance (bostøtte) is not reachable at median income, rents in Oslo are high and there is no family taxation. The main practical catch is the gap for children born in December who wait until August for a place. Norway has no earned-income credit but the wage-only minstefradrag (worth ≈ 21,000 kr per earner) and a trygdeavgift trimmed to 7.6% keep the median wedge moderate, and the Working Environment Act gives parents of under-10s a legal right to reduced hours alongside 100% sick pay from the first day.

headline.cash: 4,024 kr/month (≈ €345) tax-free barnetrygd for 2 children (2,012 kr each from 1 Feb 2026)
headline.leave: 49 weeks at 100% (15 mother + 15 father quota + 16 shared) or 61 weeks at 80%; income covered up to 6G = 819,294 kr; + 10 paid sick-child days per parent per year
headline.childcare: legal right to a place from age 1; max 1,200 kr/month (700 kr in rural municipalities), 30% off 2nd child, free from 3rd
headline.tax: foreldrefradrag: childcare costs deductible up to 25,000 kr + 15,000 kr per extra child (≈ 8,800 kr tax saved)
headline.labourtax: minstefradrag 46% of wage up to 95,700 kr (2026) + personfradrag 114,540 kr; trygdeavgift cut to 7.6%; ≈ 21,000 kr saved per earner
headline.workrights: 4 weeks + 1 day statutory leave (5 weeks by agreement) + ≈ 10 holidays; legal right to reduced hours until child is 10; 100% sick pay from day 1

policies.name: Barnehage with makspris (national fee cap)
policies.what: Legal right to a barnehage place from the month the child turns 1 (born Aug–Nov; otherwise from August). Fee capped at 1,200 kr/month since 1 Aug 2025 (700 kr in 189 least-central municipalities, free in Finnmark/Nord-Troms) plus food money; 2nd child 30% off, 3rd free; never above 6% of household income; 20 h/week free for 2–5-year-olds below 692,465 kr income.
policies.value: ≈ 2,040 kr/month (≈ €175) + food money for two full-time places; the public subsidy is ≈ 18,000–20,000 kr per place per month
policies.eligibility: All children resident in the municipality, from age 1; apply by 1 March for August intake.
policies.caveat: A child born in December waits until the next August; kontantstøtte (7,500 kr/month, months 13–19, 5 years' NI membership required) partly bridges this. Childcare costs are also deductible (foreldrefradrag, up to 25,000 + 15,000 kr/year).

policies.name: Foreldrepenger (parental benefit)
policies.what: Paid leave of 49 weeks at 100% of income or 61 weeks at 80%: 3 weeks before birth, a 15-week mother's quota, a 15-week father's quota (19 + 19 at 80%) and 16 shared weeks. Income replaced up to 6G = 819,294 kr/year (May 2026); most employers pay the excess. Father also gets 2 weeks at birth (usually paid).
